Deputy McEntee is the Minister for Defence. She is the line manager when it comes to the Army. Why is it the case that we have this level of chaos within the Cabinet that the Minister, Deputy McEntee, is not being consulted? Did the public know about the Army being called in before the Minister for Defence knew? Deputy Darren O'Rourke I attended a large public meeting in Kells last night, called for by the community in the wake of a spate of burglaries, attempted break-ins and break-ins. There is a lot of concern in the community. It was a very well-attended meeting, hosted by Oliver Figgy Curran and Councillor Michael Gallagher. Representatives of An Garda Síochána were present and took questions. A key concern that I said I would take to the Dáil today is the number of gardaí in Kells and County Meath. The figure is the lowest in all of Ireland by population. What measures are the Taoiseach and the Government taking to address the low number of gardaí in County Meath and Kells in particular? Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett I welcome the Northside Home Care Services workers in the Gallery. Deputy Murphy will be raising issues on their behalf, and I absolutely hope the Taoiseach will listen to them. I want to raise another issue. The Taoiseach probably will not know about it but I ask him to raise it with the Minister for justice. Four years ago, Ned Connors died in prison. He died of alcohol poisoning. How the alcohol got into the prison and so on is a question. There was a report done by the prison inspector into the circumstances of his death, but it still has not been published. As of today, there was supposed to be an inquest happening. His family solicitors said the inquest should not go ahead until the prison inspector’s report was published. Apparently, the Minister has for some reason prevented the report from being published. This is fuelling deep concern among the family. If the Taoiseach could ask about Ned Connors and the report into his death on behalf of his family, it would be appreciated. An Ceann Comhairle Deputy O’Rourke has the opportunity to ask another question if he wishes to exercise it. Deputy Darren O'Rourke Related to the public meeting last night to which I referred, another area is the roll-out of community CCTV, that is, the roll-out of CCTV in communities. There were restrictions in the past in terms of data protection and data management. What is the current position in relation to the roll-out of community CCTV across the State, the role of central government and the funding potentially available for that? Also, what is the role of local government in this regard? An Ceann Comhairle I apologise, Deputy Murphy was next. Deputy O’Rourke is ahead of him now anyway. Deputy Paul Murphy I thank the Ceann Comhairle. I have raised with the Taoiseach before the Northside Home Care Services workers who have been taking industrial action since January. Some of them are in the Gallery. He knows what the issue is here; it is about pay equality. Some of these workers have worked for 25 years and are getting just over €15 an hour. Others are on minimum wage and getting 30% less than others for doing the same job of providing vital care to approximately 500 people on a daily basis. What I raise today is the outrageous victimisation of their shop steward, Sonya Borwick, simply for standing up for the workers she represents. She was suspended yesterday on utterly spurious grounds. Supposedly she breached GDPR by asking people to sign a petition. She did not use any information she had about their data as a result of working there; she was simply talking to clients who support them, given the support they provide for them, asking them to sign a petition and for their address on a petition. Supposedly that is a breach of GDPR. That is blatant anti-union victimisation. I ask the Taoiseach to condemn this victimisation. Ms Borwick is in the Gallery. That she should be suspended is an action that should be utterly condemned by the Government. The Minister for Health needs to meet with these workers and instruct the HSE to treat them properly. An Ceann Comhairle The Deputy is absolutely taking liberties. I call Deputy Conway-Walsh. Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh The recent case and indeed the resilience and courage of former Garda Margaret Loftus exposed the systematic and institutionalised failures in addressing domestic, sexual and gender-based violence in Ireland, particularly when the alleged perpetrators are members of An Garda Síochána. Reliance on self-disclosure leaves systematic blind spots, allowing potential perpetrators to maintain investigative authority over other victims. Without statutory oversight, independent monitoring and systemic reform, Garda structures can shield perpetrators and undermine public confidence. I welcome the recent setting up of the dedicated domestic violence unit, but does the Taoiseach agree that the mandatory reporting of barring and protection orders is now necessary? Does he believe it is right that a garda who is convicted of breaking the law should still serve in An Garda Síochána? Deputy Gary Gannon It would be impossible to talk about the next meeting of the Cabinet committee on justice, home affairs and migration without discussing the absolute disaster that was last week. I am going to preface my comments by answering a question I know the Taoiseach will probably ask, because he asked it of my party leader earlier. Yes, I absolutely condemn the blocking of critical infrastructure and the threats to gardaí. However, does the Taoiseach endorse the tactics employed by his own Minister for justice last week, in particular the press statement that went out on Thursday morning, in advance of "Morning Ireland", stating that the Army would be on the streets and that vehicles would be damaged and nobody should complain? The Minister went on to further antagonise and accelerate an already difficult situation by saying the protesters were being manipulated by some idiot in the UK called Tommy Robinson. The C70 form sent by An Garda Síochána to the Defence Forces is an essential part of our security system. To politicise that, as the Minister for justice did on Thursday morning, is absolutely out of bounds. Does the Taoiseach endorse that? Should we see further protests on the streets, what lessons will be learned and how can we ensure it is not Government Ministers who inflame intentions? Deputy Ruth Coppinger There are calls today for an all-island response to the epidemic of gender-based violence. In Northern Ireland, 30 women have been killed since 2020. It is one of the most dangerous places in the world to be a woman. A woman is more likely to be killed by her own son than by a stranger. The family and the home are very dangerous places. ROSA in the North has called a protest in Belfast for Saturday, 25 April to respond to the fact that 30 women have been killed and to say not one more should be killed. Two women were murdered in three weeks recently. This was at the same time as the Natalie McNally trial which showed a very premeditated killing by her former partner. In relation to gender-based violence in the South, the Taoiseach mentioned legislative reform but there has been very little such reform that I can think of. The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission has added its voice to the call for access to counselling notes to be banned in gender violence trials. We need to see that legislation moved and we need to see what survivors want. Deputy Paul Lawless I could not believe my eyes when the Minister for justice outlined recently that it was his intention and the intention of the Government to introduce legislation to remove several proposed IPAS centres from the planning process entirely. I have raised this planning circumvention with the Taoiseach on a number of occasions. Both he and the Tánaiste have led the House to believe this was a temporary, emergency measure and would be removed imminently. Now we read it is the Government’s intention to make this planning exemption permanent. The IPAS system is the only accommodation system that currently avails of a planning exemption. I want the Taoiseach to be clear. What is the intention of this Government in relation to the IPAS planning exemption? Is it going to ensure that all citizens and communities are treated equally or is it going to try to continue this policy of running roughshod over communities? Is the Government going to make this planning exemption permanent? I refer to Government Deputies and backbenchers. Every time this has broken in local communities across the country, the Taoiseach has outlined that the Government wants to see community engagement and consultation with communities. This is the Taoiseach’s opportunity. What is the Taoiseach going to do? Is he going to make this permanent or will he allow communities to have a say in relation to what happens to them? The Taoiseach I thank the Deputies for raising a range of issues. Deputy Ó Murchú was first in terms of antisocial behaviour and a multi-agency approach in County Louth. I agree with the Deputy that the most effective response is a multi-agency response. I support the drug partnerships approach that we had in earlier periods. The local community safety partnership has been effective. It is working in certain locations but we need to look at further initiatives in terms of community-based partnerships on the ground that are well resourced by the State. That is a view I have. I am advocating that from my position as Taoiseach and from talking to the Ministers concerned. I thank Deputy Brabazon for raising the issue of Grace's law. It is extremely distressing and unacceptable that the Deputy and the people he represents are witnessing appalling activity by individuals using scramblers who are recklessly endangering life, causing the loss of life and so forth. I accept the rationale behind the Deputy's call for statutory indemnity to be introduced to protect members of An Garda Síochána who reasonably try to stop this activity. I do not think it is acceptable that a garda should be prosecuted if he or she is endeavouring to stop people endangering the lives of others through the illegal and reckless use of scramblers. The Minister for justice is bringing forward some form of review of the legislation in this area. This is a very important issue because if something is not done, the potential is that we will paralyse the Garda in terms of protecting people. I will talk to the Minister for justice. I know he is minded to do something in this area in light of recent court cases. I will liaise back with Deputy Brabazon on this. I heard what Deputy Tóibín had to say. In the first instance, C70 requests made very regularly. About 140 were issued last year. Last week, a request was made with a view to calling in the Army to tow big lorries and trucks away from vital critical infrastructure. I do not know whether the Deputy condemns or agrees with the blockading of an oil refinery. I saw his posts all week. He supported the blockade of the oil refinery----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín It was not----- The Taoiseach The Deputy did so. He went on the platform----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín You are not telling the truth. The Taoiseach You went on the platform and you supported the blockade of the motorway. The Deputy supported the blockades of ports. All I would say to him is----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín There is a weakness in your argument. If you cannot tell the truth, then it is a weakness. An Ceann Comhairle Deputy, do not use that type of inference. You can write to the Taoiseach. This is not a forum for back and forth; this is Taoiseach's questions. You ask a question. If you do not like the answer, you write to the Taoiseach. End of story. Deputy Peadar Tóibín It is not that I do not like the answer; it is untrue. An Ceann Comhairle That is i t. End of story. We conform to the rules. Deputy Peadar Tóibín It is not the truth. The Taoiseach I did watch the Deputy's social media posts. He described it as mediating, but who gives him authority to decide who gets oil in this country? Who gives him authority----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín The Taoiseach is asking me a question. An Ceann Comhairle No, he is not. The Taoiseach I am asking a rhetorical question. I do not need a response right now. I am making an absolutely fundamental point with regard to parliamentary democracy. The Deputy does not have a right to decide who gets access to work. He does not have a right to decide who gets access to a hospital. He does not have a right to----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín There are nearly 1 million people on the hospital waiting lists. An Ceann Comhairle Every other Member needs a fair amount of time. The Taoiseach It was wrong of the Deputy to do what he did last week. I say that respectfully to him. No self-appointed group gets that right and no TD gets that right. A number of TDs were at that. Deputy Tóibín, more than most, stated that he had negotiated this or negotiated that. That is not right. For God's sake----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín We negotiated----- The Taoiseach -----we need freedom of movement for people. The Minister for justice and the Minister for----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín Did the public know? An Ceann Comhairle Deputy, that is enough. The Taoiseach -----Defence engage with each other in respect of this issue. Deputy O'Rourke raised two issues on the concerns in Navan----- Deputy Darren O'Rourke In Kells. The Taoiseach In Kells. My apologies. The Deputy raised concerns about break-ins and burglaries. I will relay that to the Minister for justice. I am sure the Garda will tackle that in a concerted way. That is very disturbing for the people concerned. Garda numbers are improving every time a new intake goes through Templemore. As a result, I expect that we will be able to get there. We have done good work in Dublin, Cork, Limerick and other locations. As more gardaí come through, we are trying to get to as many areas as we possibly can in sufficient numbers, not just giving dribs and drabs, in order that we get good solid allocations. The Deputy also raised the issue of community CCTV. I will have to get an update on that. It continues to be very effective and impactful in combating crime. Deputy Paul Murphy referred to the Northside Home Care Service workers, as did Deputy Boyd Barrett. I am not familiar with the background to the suspension of the shop steward. I will ask for that to be investigated and checked by the Minister for Health. I am not saying that this justifies suspension, but I would be wary of using clients to sign petitions. I understand how it happens, because people need the service and people want the service to be supported. I will talk to the Minister about the general issue. Those involved were here a number of weeks ago as well, and this issue needs to be resolved. The process should be deal with through labour relations in order to get it resolved. Meanwhile, the atmosphere around this should be one that allows engagement and so forth. Deputy Boyd Barrett also raised the issue of Ned Connors, who died in prison through alcohol poisoning. That is very disturbing. The Deputy said "Apparently, the Minister has for some reason prevented the report from being published." The Minister for justice, Deputy O'Callaghan, is a fair-minded person and is scrupulous----- Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett Something has stalled the report. An Ceann Comhairle No, Deputy. The Taoiseach The Minister is scrupulous in terms of the application of the law. I do not know what the background is to this. Maybe they do not want to prejudice the process. I do not know. I will check with the Minister for justice in respect of the report. I think the inquest is due, is it not? Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett Yes. The Taoiseach Deputy Conway Walsh raised the issue of a former garda, Margaret Loftus, and members of An Garda Síochána. Again, there has to be clear rules in terms of our uniformed services, particularly our Garda and our military. There are rules in respect of people who are convicted of crimes. They should not serve. When people are charged, they are sometimes suspended pending the outcome of the investigation and so forth. I salute the courage of Margaret Loftus. On the mandatory reporting of barring orders, I would like a report back on that. I think the Minister is working on something in that regard. To be fair to him, Deputy Gannon condemned blockading. With regard to the decision that was made, we had to remove those vehicles from Whitegate. We simply had to. I got a phone call to say that the refinery was closing. That would have been ruinous for the country because one cannot restart a refinery straight away. How bad would that have been. The Minister for justice made the correct decision in asking the Army in because it has the equipment to remove big lorries, tractors and other machines. It would have been crazy if we ended up stopping the export oil from Whitegate. An Ceann Comhairle There are two more Deputies, Taoiseach. The Taoiseach It just would not have made any sense, and that is why it was done. On Deputy Coppinger's question, through the shared island initiative, we support an all-island response to domestic and sexual violence. It is shocking, and Northern Ireland is a particular problem. I have discussed this with the First Minister and deputy First Minister at meetings of the North-South Ministerial Council. It was a theme and a topic at our most recent meeting. There is active co-operation to the effect that there should be a joint approach between our Government and the Executive in respect of domestic and sexual violence. It is a big worry. Deputy Coppinger reminded us of the 30 women who have been killed. That is shocking and wrong. With regard to the counselling notes, the Minister for justice is bringing forward legislation in which he will go as he possibly can to place real conditions on the use of counselling notes. On Deputy Lawless' question, the Government has huge pressures. I gave the figures earlier. We are making a lot of progress in terms of a more rigorous, timely and efficient response to those seeking asylum. Nonetheless, people come into the country to seek asylum. They are legally entitled to seek asylum and our job is to process applications as quickly as we can. If people are entitled to asylum, they get it. If they are not, they should be deported or asked to leave. Deputy Paul Lawless The question is----- An Ceann Comhairle No. The Taoiseach The question is this. I am asking the Deputy his view. As they come into the country on a daily basis, where should people stay? Should they be on the streets? What is the solution? An Ceann Comhairle No, we are out of time. The Deputy can request the information in writing. The Taoiseach We are under international legal obligations. This is a challenge----- An Ceann Comhairle The Deputy can write to the Taoiseach.. Deputy Paul Lawless The question relates to planning. An Ceann Comhairle Thank you, Taoiseach. We are out of time. The Taoiseach We do not have time now to discuss it, but I would gladly discuss it with the Deputy again. An Ceann Comhairle That concludes Taoiseach's Questions. An Ceann Comhairle The Deputy is fully entitled. We are finished.

This was an increase of €12 million compared with the previous year. Among other items, the Cabinet committee also oversees the development and delivery of the whole-of-government response to migration and integration, including through a national migration and integration strategy. The new International Protection Bill 2026 will give effect to the measures of the European Union migration and asylum pact. Enactment of the Bill and commencement of the Act is required by 12 June 2026. To prepare for its introduction, a phased transition that mirrors elements of the pact is currently under way. As part of this, applicants from designated safe countries of origin, including Nigeria, and in the context of the Dublin III regulation and inadmissible cases, are being processed under these new processes, with some minor exceptions. As of 24 March 2026, 1,280 applications were received under the accelerated process. Of these, 80% have received a first instance decision. Decisions were negative in 88% of cases, with an 11% grant rate and a number of withdrawals. Of those with a negative decision, 48% appealed and 86% of appeals were refused. A total of 482 deportation orders has been issued, with seven enforced removals and 42 voluntary returns having taken place. The median timeline from application to enforced removal was 24 weeks, and 15 weeks for voluntary return. This indicates the pact programme can meet the future timelines for the border procedure. The number of international protection applications has been rising over the past number of years, reaching 18,500 in 2024. In 2025, application numbers reduced by approximately one third. In 2025, the International Protection Office delivered over 20,200 first decisions compared with approximately 14,000 in 2024, which is a 44% increase. The International Protection Appeals Tribunal more than doubled the number of appeals closed, from 3,100 in 2024 to nearly 6,320 in 2025. In addition to meetings of the Cabinet committee, I have regular engagements with Ministers at Cabinet and individually to discuss issues relating to their Departments. An Ceann Comhairle A lot of Members are seeking to contribute. They have one minute each. I call Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú. Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú Louth County Council is trying to update its tenant engagement and antisocial behaviour strategy, and I sat in yesterday for a short period on a consultative event. It is all about having a multiagency approach, strengthening community safety, embedding tenant engagement for the first time, improving well-being and neighbourhood cohesion and ensuring fairness, transparency and accountability. That is all sound. This is a continuation, however, of an issue I have brought up before. I think we have to be really serious in relation to the complex issues involved. I am sure many of us will have dealt with local authorities, the Garda and others in this context. The fact is we have to get very serious. I do not believe the community safety partnership is going to quite bridge the gap, however much I would like to think it would. I am thinking of Barrack Street in Dundalk. An Ceann Comhairle Is there a question? Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú Yes. This is about how we can get to having a proper, multiagency approach to deal with the complexity and early intervention and policing aspects. Deputy Tom Brabazon I welcome the recent introduction of Grace’s Law, the intention of which is to make scramblers illegal in public places. However, these vehicles are still causing havoc in my community and in communities across the northside of Dublin. To combat this, I am asking that a statutory indemnity be introduced for gardaí pursuing scramblers and acting within reason so they can carry out their duty without fear or favour to ensure our communities can be protected. Will the Government now commit to introducing a statutory indemnity or some other statutory mechanism so members of An Garda Síochána who are going about their work in a reasonable way will be protected from prosecution? Deputy Peadar Tóibín One of the most controversial elements of the omnishambles of last week was the threat of the Garda and the Army. The Minister, Deputy O’Callaghan, spoke to the Tánaiste and Taoiseach about utilising the Army for Whitegate refinery on Wednesday, 8 April. The next day, the Minister made public that a request was being made to the Defence Forces. The Minister, Deputy McEntee, was not informed until just before the request went in. Deputy McEntee is the Minister for Defence. She is the line manager when it comes to the Army. Why is it the case that we have this level of chaos within the Cabinet that the Minister, Deputy McEntee, is not being consulted? Did the public know about the Army being called in before the Minister for Defence knew? Representatives of An Garda Síochána were present and took questions. A key concern that I said I would take to the Dáil today is the number of gardaí in Kells and County Meath. Deputy Murphy will be raising issues on their behalf, and I absolutely hope the Taoiseach will listen to them. I want to raise another issue. The Taoiseach probably will not know about it but I ask him to raise it with the Minister for justice. Four years ago, Ned Connors died in prison. He died of alcohol poisoning. How the alcohol got into the prison and so on is a question. There was a report done by the prison inspector into the circumstances of his death, but it still has not been published. As of today, there was supposed to be an inquest happening. His family solicitors said the inquest should not go ahead until the prison inspector’s report was published. Apparently, the Minister has for some reason prevented the report from being published. This is fuelling deep concern among the family. If the Taoiseach could ask about Ned Connors and the report into his death on behalf of his family, it would be appreciated. An Ceann Comhairle Deputy O’Rourke has the opportunity to ask another question if he wishes to exercise it. Deputy Darren O'Rourke Related to the public meeting last night to which I referred, another area is the roll-out of community CCTV, that is, the roll-out of CCTV in communities. There were restrictions in the past in terms of data protection and data management. What is the current position in relation to the roll-out of community CCTV across the State, the role of central government and the funding potentially available for that? Some of them are in the Gallery. He knows what the issue is here; it is about pay equality. Some of these workers have worked for 25 years and are getting just over €15 an hour. Others are on minimum wage and getting 30% less than others for doing the same job of providing vital care to approximately 500 people on a daily basis. Supposedly that is a breach of GDPR. That is blatant anti-union victimisation. I ask the Taoiseach to condemn this victimisation. Ms Borwick is in the Gallery. That she should be suspended is an action that should be utterly condemned by the Government. The Minister for Health needs to meet with these workers and instruct the HSE to treat them properly. An Ceann Comhairle The Deputy is absolutely taking liberties. I call Deputy Conway-Walsh. Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh The recent case and indeed the resilience and courage of former Garda Margaret Loftus exposed the systematic and institutionalised failures in addressing domestic, sexual and gender-based violence in Ireland, particularly when the alleged perpetrators are members of An Garda Síochána. Reliance on self-disclosure leaves systematic blind spots, allowing potential perpetrators to maintain investigative authority over other victims. Without statutory oversight, independent monitoring and systemic reform, Garda structures can shield perpetrators and undermine public confidence. I welcome the recent setting up of the dedicated domestic violence unit, but does the Taoiseach agree that the mandatory reporting of barring and protection orders is now necessary? Does he believe it is right that a garda who is convicted of breaking the law should still serve in An Garda Síochána? Deputy Gary Gannon It would be impossible to talk about the next meeting of the Cabinet committee on justice, home affairs and migration without discussing the absolute disaster that was last week. Yes, I absolutely condemn the blocking of critical infrastructure and the threats to gardaí. Deputy Ruth Coppinger There are calls today for an all-island response to the epidemic of gender-based violence. In Northern Ireland, 30 women have been killed since 2020. An Ceann Comhairle Every other Member needs a fair amount of time. The Taoiseach It was wrong of the Deputy to do what he did last week. I say that respectfully to him. The Minister for justice and the Minister for----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín Did the public know? An Ceann Comhairle Deputy, that is enough. An Ceann Comhairle The Deputy is fully entitled. We are finished.

Does he believe it is right that a garda who is convicted of breaking the law should still serve in An Garda Síochána? Deputy Gary Gannon It would be impossible to talk about the next meeting of the Cabinet committee on justice, home affairs and migration without discussing the absolute disaster that was last week. I am going to preface my comments by answering a question I know the Taoiseach will probably ask, because he asked it of my party leader earlier. Yes, I absolutely condemn the blocking of critical infrastructure and the threats to gardaí. However, does the Taoiseach endorse the tactics employed by his own Minister for justice last week, in particular the press statement that went out on Thursday morning, in advance of "Morning Ireland", stating that the Army would be on the streets and that vehicles would be damaged and nobody should complain? The Minister went on to further antagonise and accelerate an already difficult situation by saying the protesters were being manipulated by some idiot in the UK called Tommy Robinson. The C70 form sent by An Garda Síochána to the Defence Forces is an essential part of our security system. To politicise that, as the Minister for justice did on Thursday morning, is absolutely out of bounds. Does the Taoiseach endorse that? Should we see further protests on the streets, what lessons will be learned and how can we ensure it is not Government Ministers who inflame intentions? Deputy Ruth Coppinger There are calls today for an all-island response to the epidemic of gender-based violence. In Northern Ireland, 30 women have been killed since 2020. It is one of the most dangerous places in the world to be a woman. A woman is more likely to be killed by her own son than by a stranger. The family and the home are very dangerous places. ROSA in the North has called a protest in Belfast for Saturday, 25 April to respond to the fact that 30 women have been killed and to say not one more should be killed. Two women were murdered in three weeks recently. This was at the same time as the Natalie McNally trial which showed a very premeditated killing by her former partner. In relation to gender-based violence in the South, the Taoiseach mentioned legislative reform but there has been very little such reform that I can think of. The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission has added its voice to the call for access to counselling notes to be banned in gender violence trials. We need to see that legislation moved and we need to see what survivors want. Deputy Paul Lawless I could not believe my eyes when the Minister for justice outlined recently that it was his intention and the intention of the Government to introduce legislation to remove several proposed IPAS centres from the planning process entirely. I have raised this planning circumvention with the Taoiseach on a number of occasions. Both he and the Tánaiste have led the House to believe this was a temporary, emergency measure and would be removed imminently. Now we read it is the Government’s intention to make this planning exemption permanent. The IPAS system is the only accommodation system that currently avails of a planning exemption. I want the Taoiseach to be clear. What is the intention of this Government in relation to the IPAS planning exemption? Is it going to ensure that all citizens and communities are treated equally or is it going to try to continue this policy of running roughshod over communities? Is the Government going to make this planning exemption permanent? I refer to Government Deputies and backbenchers. Every time this has broken in local communities across the country, the Taoiseach has outlined that the Government wants to see community engagement and consultation with communities. This is the Taoiseach’s opportunity. What is the Taoiseach going to do? Is he going to make this permanent or will he allow communities to have a say in relation to what happens to them? The Taoiseach I thank the Deputies for raising a range of issues. Deputy Ó Murchú was first in terms of antisocial behaviour and a multi-agency approach in County Louth. I agree with the Deputy that the most effective response is a multi-agency response. I support the drug partnerships approach that we had in earlier periods. The local community safety partnership has been effective. It is working in certain locations but we need to look at further initiatives in terms of community-based partnerships on the ground that are well resourced by the State. That is a view I have. I am advocating that from my position as Taoiseach and from talking to the Ministers concerned. I thank Deputy Brabazon for raising the issue of Grace's law. It is extremely distressing and unacceptable that the Deputy and the people he represents are witnessing appalling activity by individuals using scramblers who are recklessly endangering life, causing the loss of life and so forth. I accept the rationale behind the Deputy's call for statutory indemnity to be introduced to protect members of An Garda Síochána who reasonably try to stop this activity. I do not think it is acceptable that a garda should be prosecuted if he or she is endeavouring to stop people endangering the lives of others through the illegal and reckless use of scramblers. The Minister for justice is bringing forward some form of review of the legislation in this area. This is a very important issue because if something is not done, the potential is that we will paralyse the Garda in terms of protecting people. I will talk to the Minister for justice. I know he is minded to do something in this area in light of recent court cases. I will liaise back with Deputy Brabazon on this. I heard what Deputy Tóibín had to say. In the first instance, C70 requests made very regularly. About 140 were issued last year. Last week, a request was made with a view to calling in the Army to tow big lorries and trucks away from vital critical infrastructure. I do not know whether the Deputy condemns or agrees with the blockading of an oil refinery. I saw his posts all week. He supported the blockade of the oil refinery----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín It was not----- The Taoiseach The Deputy did so. He went on the platform----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín You are not telling the truth. The Taoiseach You went on the platform and you supported the blockade of the motorway. The Deputy supported the blockades of ports. All I would say to him is----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín There is a weakness in your argument. If you cannot tell the truth, then it is a weakness. An Ceann Comhairle Deputy, do not use that type of inference. You can write to the Taoiseach. This is not a forum for back and forth; this is Taoiseach's questions. You ask a question. If you do not like the answer, you write to the Taoiseach. End of story. Deputy Peadar Tóibín It is not that I do not like the answer; it is untrue. An Ceann Comhairle That is i t. End of story. We conform to the rules. Deputy Peadar Tóibín It is not the truth. The Taoiseach I did watch the Deputy's social media posts. He described it as mediating, but who gives him authority to decide who gets oil in this country? Who gives him authority----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín The Taoiseach is asking me a question. An Ceann Comhairle No, he is not. The Taoiseach I am asking a rhetorical question. I do not need a response right now. I am making an absolutely fundamental point with regard to parliamentary democracy. The Deputy does not have a right to decide who gets access to work. He does not have a right to decide who gets access to a hospital. He does not have a right to----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín There are nearly 1 million people on the hospital waiting lists. An Ceann Comhairle Every other Member needs a fair amount of time. The Taoiseach It was wrong of the Deputy to do what he did last week. I say that respectfully to him. No self-appointed group gets that right and no TD gets that right. A number of TDs were at that. Deputy Tóibín, more than most, stated that he had negotiated this or negotiated that. That is not right. For God's sake----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín We negotiated----- The Taoiseach -----we need freedom of movement for people. The Minister for justice and the Minister for----- Deputy Peadar Tóibín Did the public know? An Ceann Comhairle Deputy, that is enough. The Taoiseach -----Defence engage with each other in respect of this issue. Deputy O'Rourke raised two issues on the concerns in Navan----- Deputy Darren O'Rourke In Kells. The Taoiseach In Kells. My apologies. The Deputy raised concerns about break-ins and burglaries. I will relay that to the Minister for justice. I am sure the Garda will tackle that in a concerted way. That is very disturbing for the people concerned. Garda numbers are improving every time a new intake goes through Templemore. As a result, I expect that we will be able to get there. We have done good work in Dublin, Cork, Limerick and other locations. As more gardaí come through, we are trying to get to as many areas as we possibly can in sufficient numbers, not just giving dribs and drabs, in order that we get good solid allocations. The Deputy also raised the issue of community CCTV. I will have to get an update on that. It continues to be very effective and impactful in combating crime. Deputy Paul Murphy referred to the Northside Home Care Service workers, as did Deputy Boyd Barrett. I am not familiar with the background to the suspension of the shop steward. I will ask for that to be investigated and checked by the Minister for Health. I am not saying that this justifies suspension, but I would be wary of using clients to sign petitions. I understand how it happens, because people need the service and people want the service to be supported. I will talk to the Minister about the general issue. Those involved were here a number of weeks ago as well, and this issue needs to be resolved. The process should be deal with through labour relations in order to get it resolved. If they are not, they should be deported or asked to leave. Deputy Paul Lawless The question is----- An Ceann Comhairle No. The Taoiseach The question is this. I am asking the Deputy his view. As they come into the country on a daily basis, where should people stay? Should they be on the streets? What is the solution? An Ceann Comhairle No, we are out of time. The Deputy can request the information in writing. The Taoiseach We are under international legal obligations. This is a challenge----- An Ceann Comhairle The Deputy can write to the Taoiseach.. Deputy Paul Lawless The question relates to planning. An Ceann Comhairle Thank you, Taoiseach. We are out of time. The Taoiseach We do not have time now to discuss it, but I would gladly discuss it with the Deputy again. An Ceann Comhairle That concludes Taoiseach's Questions. An Ceann Comhairle The Deputy is fully entitled. We are finished.

question: 227. question: 283. Deputy Holly Cairns asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he is aware of instances of fridges being removed from residents in IPAS centres; and if ample consideration is given to and provision made for, vulnerable people with medically mandated dietary requirements or medicines which may require refrigeration (details supplied). [27369/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration While the Department can't provide information about individual cases, this matter has been raised with officials who are giving it attention. IPAS Accommodation is provided in a range of different locations and types of accommodation, including both self-catering and catered accommodation. As per the IPAS House Rules, the use of unauthorised electrical equipment such as fridges in residents’ rooms in some centres is not permitted, because of the significant fire and health and safety risks they pose. IPAS directs centres, where necessary, to provide a fridge in a shared space or add a secure box to a shared fridge for medicines which may require refrigeration. Where there are medically mandated dietary requirements, the resident can inform centre management in order for them to provide for this appropriately. If a person applying for international protection has any concerns in relation to their accommodation, they can also contact IPAS directly via a dedicated helpdesk at ipasinbox@justice.ie .

question: 284. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department has considered any proposals to ban online gambling advertising; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [27481/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 284 and 289 together. The Gambling Regulation Act 2024 (‘Act of 2024’) contains provisions in relation to the advertising of gambling activities, including online and on social media. The Act of 2024 established a new, dedicated, independent statutory authority – Údarás Rialála Cearrbhachais na hÉireann, the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (the ‘Authority’) – to regulate the gambling sector. The provisions of the Act and the powers of the Authority are being rolled out on a phased basis. Earlier this year I signed a commencement order which allowed the Authority to begin accepting and processing applications for remote and in-person betting licences, in line with the Act of 2024, from 5 February 2026. As the Authority builds up its resources, commencement of the licensing of the gaming and lotteries sector will next take place. The advertising provisions of the Act of 2024 mostly apply to those licensed by the Authority. The Act provides for a number of safeguards to protect people, most notably children and vulnerable persons from the harms associated with gambling, with a particular focus on online activities. These measures include section 146 which provides that advertising of gambling activities on social media or video-sharing services may only be permitted where a person has an account on a social media or video sharing service and has specifically subscribed to a licensee’s account on that service and section 149 which provides for a watershed prohibiting gambling advertising between 5:30 am to 9 pm on audio-visual on-demand media services, on-demand sound services and broadcasters. Section 144 provides for a wide-ranging power to allow the Authority to prescribe the times, place and events where gambling advertising can be broadcast, displayed or published, and allows the Authority to specify the frequency which advertising can be shown or broadcast and the duration of such advertisements. The Act also includes a number of provisions dedicated to protecting children offline. Section 151 prohibits the manufacture, import for sale in the State, or the sale or supply (including free of charge) of branded clothing or merchandise, by a licensee, that are intended to be worn or used by children. Furthermore, section 159 of the Act prohibits a licensee from sponsoring or causing another person to sponsor: - an event or part of an event where the majority or participants or attendees are children. - an event aimed at children; - an organisation, club or team that has children as members; - a premises that is used by an organisation, club or team that has children as members; or - a public activity that appeals to children. These sections have not been commenced as yet. The protections and safeguards provided for in the Act are contingent on the majority of the sector being licensed and regulated by the Authority. Officials in my Department are continuing to work, in collaboration with the Authority, on progressing the further commencement of the remaining provisions of the Act as quickly as possible.

question: 286. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason a person’s naturalisation process is taking so long (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [27366/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants. I want to assure anyone who has an application for naturalisation submitted that the Citizenship Division of my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible. It is important to note, however, that no two naturalisation applications are the same and some take longer than others to process. Given the importance of citizenship, robust and comprehensive checks must take place on each application. Unfortunately, some checks, such as international checks, can take a considerable amount of time and these are largely outside of the control of the Immigration Service. For that reason, while, I expect that going forward, that most applicants will receive a decision within one year, this cannot be guaranteed in the case of applications made in any specific year. Citizenship Division have taken a significant number of steps to improve the process for applicants. These included introducing an online digital application, online payments, and the introduction of eVetting. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that these changes are reducing processing times. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 287. Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason there has been a significant delay in delivering the recommendations in the Garda Vetting Review in 2021; when these recommendations will be implemented; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [27406/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. The Interdepartmental Vetting Review Group was chaired by my Department and comprised representatives of the following Departments and Agencies: • An Garda Síochána • Tusla • Public Appointments Service • Department of Education • Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth • Department of Housing, Planning and Local Government • Health Service Executive • Department of Foreign Affairs. The initial focus of the Group's work was the introduction of a system for re-vetting, as well as a review of the approach to vetting for specific employments, to streamline, as far as possible, the administrative arrangements, without compromising the safety of children and vulnerable adults. As the group moved ahead with its work, additional issues were raised and considered. The group took a careful and thorough approach, as was necessary in meeting its aim of ensuring that the vetting system remains robust and effective as a crucial safeguard for the most vulnerable members of society, that is children and vulnerable adults, while also improving the service to customers. Ultimately, although the group did not agree a report, I was provided with details of its work and it is clear that aspects of the current vetting system result in a highly-segmented process. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the necessary high standards for this process. I have therefore directed that steps be taken to implement a number of key changes, specifically in relation to re-vetting and the portability of vetting. In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, that individual would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category. These changes will require amending legislation and updated technical systems to support the revised approach, to make the process more efficient for volunteers and organisations, without compromising the essential safeguards that protect those in our care. My Department continues to engage with the Garda National Vetting Bureau on the detailed work of developing the necessary legislative and technical steps to meet these goals in a way that is workable in practice. It is my objective to ensure that the vetting system is fit for purpose and, to the greatest extent possible, efficient and future-proofed to continue to protect our children and vulnerable adults.

question: 288. Deputy Holly Cairns asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if data is available on the number and type of complaints made under Coco's law; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [27412/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Harassment, Harmful Communications and Related Offences Act 2020, also known as Coco’s Law, came into force in February 2021. The Act criminalises the sharing of, or threatening to share, intimate images without a person’s consent, with or without intent to cause harm to the victim. The Act also seeks to target other areas of harmful communications by creating a new offence of distributing, publishing, or sending a threatening or grossly offensive communication with intent to cause harm and to extend the current offence of harassment to deal with communications about a person, as well as communications to a person. An Garda Síochána has advised that there are three different incident types captured on the PULSE recording system under the Harassment, Harmful Communications and Related Offences Act 2020. Those are: Distributing grossly offensive communication. Distributing/publishing/recording intimate image(s). Recoding intimate image(s) causing interference/alarm. The attached table offers a breakdown of these incidents from February 2021 to date. All information contained in this response is based upon operational data from the PULSE system as was available on 1 April 2026. Figures that are less than 10 are reported as “<10” in line with An Garda Síochána Analysis Services (GSAS) reporting standards. Table 1

question: 293. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for a list of all proposed or planned International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres in Mullingar, Athlone and the wider Midlands region, and nationally; the current status of each proposed centre; the expected capacity of each; and the anticipated timelines for opening, in tabular form. [27603/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 293, 294, 295, 296 and 297 together. I understand from the Deputy's questions that her question relates to new proposed or planned accommodation centres in the areas mentioned. The Department receives regular offers of accommodation from external providers and does not predetermine their geographical location. All offers of accommodation are reviewed by the Department under a standard appraisal procedure. The Department is not currently considering offers from any properties in Mullingar, Athlone, or the wider Midlands region for use as international protection accommodation. In relation to existing accommodation centres in the area, the Department’s Community Engagement Team (CET) was established to engage directly with elected representatives, relevant Local Authorities, Local Development Companies, and other entities and individuals around the time of opening new IPAS accommodation centres and Ukraine accommodation. The team aims to improve the flow of information regarding arrivals into areas and to help equip local communities with accurate information, and to assist with the welcome and integration process for new arrivals. From January 2024 to date, the Community Engagement Team issued formal briefing notes regarding the opening of two accommodation centres for people seeking international protection in Co. Westmeath to local elected representatives and the local authorities. The team also links with other stakeholders outside of immediate openings of centres to build relationships and networks with key groups. This includes meetings with Community Integration Fora, Local Development Companies (LDCs) and other non-governmental organisations. The team engages with central government Departments and local services to provide information to assist with planning and activation of services. The Community Engagement Team has presented to Westmeath County Council on their work and met with the Westmeath Community Integration Forum on a number of occasions since being established. Different sites have different engagement needs and the team aims to be flexible to meet the needs of the community. Many communities are working with the team on openings of centres across the country and are happy to manage and facilitate new arrivals themselves with support from local authorities, local development companies or indeed other community groups. We are grateful for this support. For example, the LDC in Westmeath supported the CET to convene four meetings with community groups in advance of the opening of the accommodation centre at Harry’s Hotel, Kinnegad. The CET also met with local elected representatives on two occasions as well as providing information in response to queries received through the team’s dedicated mailbox. There has been extended engagement in the case of State-owned sites, like Midlands Accommodation Centre (MAC) and Citywest Accommodation Centre. In the case of MAC, the CET proactively engaged to ensure that local elected representatives and local stakeholders were informed of the plans and developments at the site. After informing local elected representatives that the Department intended to develop the site for accommodation for people seeking international protection, the CET published a dedicated webpage to ensure that local stakeholders had access to accurate information about the development and began to convene meetings with stakeholders. While legal proceedings impacted on the centre development and engagement plans, between October 2024 and November 2025 the CET Team issued five information updates to local elected representatives and held 18 meetings with local stakeholders including local elected representatives and community members. The centre was decanted of all residents in November 2025, but remains part of the Department's strategy in relation to providing accommodation on State-owned lands.

question: 271. Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Taoiseach when the Cabinet Committee on Justice, Migration and Social Affairs will next meet. [27002/26]
answer: The Taoiseach The Cabinet Committee on Justice, Migration and Social Affairs oversees the implementation of Programme for Government commitments that are in relation to matters under those areas. It was established in February 2025 following the appointment of the new Government in January. Its first meeting was on 10th April 2025 and met most recently on February 9th 2026. The next meeting is scheduled for later this month. The Cabinet Committee covers a range of policy areas, including Domestic, Sexual and Gender Based Violence, policing and justice reform, migration and initiatives tackling local area disadvantage. Amongst other items, it also oversees the development and delivery of the whole of Government response to migration and integration, including through a National Migration and Integration Strategy. In addition to meetings of the Cabinet Committee, I have regular engagements with Ministers at Cabinet and individually to discuss issues relating to their Departments.

question: 341. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her views on a statement issued by the Government on 10 December 2025 (details supplied), specifically regarding its proposals to shift the interpretation of the ECHR specifically in relation to Articles 8 and 3 as they pertain to the deportation of persons to potentially dangerous or oppressive conditions; the position regarding the ECHR and penal exile; her views on the bearing that the statement has on the position regarding treatment of 'the Hooded Men' and interned persons during the troubles; her views on the interpretation of the ECHR; and if Oireachtas Éireann will be briefed, consulted, and its support sought in relation to Government support for a political declaration at the next committee of Ministers in Europe on matters relating to the interpretation of European Convention Rights; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [26980/26]
answer: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Ireland’s support for the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and the role of the European Court of Human Rights as essential elements of the architecture of the rule of law in Europe is firm and longstanding. Our support for the Council of Europe’s essential role in promoting human rights, democracy and the rule of law across Europe continues. The government continues to advocate for and fully respect the independence and integrity of the Court, the maintaining and upholding of the Convention and respect for the universality of human rights. At the same time, the Government believes it is important to acknowledge that there have been growing concerns among Member States of the Council of Europe about ensuring a fair and effective migration system, while fully respecting the integrity of the ECHR. With a view to promoting effective multilateralism, we consider it important that such discussions take place within the institutional framework of the Council of Europe, and this view is widely shared by Member States. An informal Justice Ministerial Conference was thus held in Strasbourg on 10 December 2025 to address these concerns. The statement with which Ireland and 26 other Member States aligned at that conference, flagged challenges faced by Member States in the context of migration and expulsion of persons of foreign nationality who have committed an offence. It also noted also Member States’ commitment to international law and the European Convention of Human Rights as a cornerstone of this international order and their support for the work and independence of the European Court of Human Rights and its jurisdiction as defined in the Convention. On foot of that conference, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe instructed the Steering Committee for Human Rights to prepare elements for a political declaration reaffirming the obligation to ensure the effective enjoyment of the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the European Convention on Human Rights to everyone within the jurisdiction of member States in the context of the contemporary challenges posed both by irregular migration and by the situation of foreigners convicted of serious offences, taking duly into account in particular governments’ fundamental responsibility to ensure national security and public safety. As per the terms of its mandate, the Steering Committee for Human Rights reported back to the Committee of Ministers on 20 March 2026. The Minister’s Deputies are now in the process of finalising the declaration to be submitted for adoption at the 135th Session of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe, which is to take place in Moldova on 14-15 May 2026. Article 3 of the Convention provides that no one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. This prohibition is absolute. It permits no derogation, contains no exceptions, and allows for no legitimate interference. Article 8, paragraph one of the Convention provides that everyone has the right to respect for his private and family life, his home and his correspondence. Article 8, paragraph two of the Convention provides that there shall be no interference by a public authority with the exercise of this right except such as is in accordance with the law and is necessary in a democratic society in the interests of national security, public safety or the economic well-being of the country, for the prevention of disorder or crime, for the protection of health or morals, or for the protection of the rights and freedoms of others. Ireland is closely following developments on this issue and engaging constructively with other Member States of the Council of Europe with a view to achieving a consensus around a political declaration fully consistent with and respectful of the Convention, including the absolute prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading or punishment contained in Article 3. Regarding the possible bearing of the 10 December 2025 joint statement on the position regarding interned persons during the Troubles and the Ireland v UK (1978. 2018) cases, it is considered that the joint statement does not alter the State’s position on these issues. The reference to Article 3 and inhuman and degrading treatment in the December joint statement is stated to be related to States’ ability to take proportionate decisions on the expulsion of persons of foreign nationality who have committed an offence, or in removal or extradition cases. The Programme for Government states explicitly that we remain steadfast in implementing the Good Friday Agreement in full. The significance of the ECHR as a core safeguard of the Good Friday Agreement is well recognised by this Government and I am unwavering in my determination to maintain that protection. I see multilateralism as essential to protect human rights, democracy and the rule of law. This is why our support for the Council of Europe remains strong. The process of finalising a political declaration at the next session of the Committee of Ministers allows us to address the challenges being experienced by many member states, while recognising the independence and impartiality of the European Court of Human Rights. The Government will keep the Oireachtas informed of developments in this matter.

question: 742. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Transport the analysis has been carried out regarding the effect on elderly residents, isolated rural communities, and individuals placed in Direct Provision or emergency accommodation; the way in which people who rely on the route 52 service for shopping, family visits, sporting events, and community activities will be supported; if the NTA has identified the number of rural towns/villages will be left with no public transport at all; and the measures that will be introduced to prevent rural isolation as a result of this cancellation. [25475/26]
answer: Minister for Transport I propose to take Questions Nos. 736, 738, 740, 741, 742, 743, 744 and 745 together. As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations of public transport. Bus Éireann operates both Public Service Obligation services funded by the State subvention and Expressway intercity services which operate on a commercial basis and do not receive any State subvention. I am aware that Bus Éireann recently announced the withdrawal of some services which operate under its Expressway service. This decision was taken following a financial and operational review carried out by Bus Éireann with regard Expressway performance over recent years, which sought to ensure the long-term financial sustainability of the company as a whole. As is the case with any such commercial route withdrawals, the withdrawal of these routes has now triggered the NTA’s PSO Determination process, and a decision will issue on this soon. Therefore, as the query raised by the Deputy is a commercial operational matter for Bus Éireann, I have referred the Deputy's question to the company for direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within ten working days.

question: 808. Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Transport when the statutory fee for the release of a vehicle detained under the Road Traffic Act 1994 was last reviewed; whether his Department has engaged with the Department of Justice; Home Affairs and Migration or An Garda Síochána regarding the adequacy of the current €125 fee as a deterrent; and whether he will consider amending the relevant regulations to provide for an increased or graduated fee structure. [26261/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Transport I propose to take Questions Nos. 807 and 808 together. The Road Traffic Act 1994 (Detention of Vehicles) Regulations 2011 (SI 460/2011) sets out An Garda Síochána's powers to detain mechanically propelled vehicles in use in a public place. These regulations were made following consultation with the Minister for Justice. Under Regulation 3, a Garda may, for reasons set out in Section 41 of the 1994 Act, detain, remove and store a vehicle. Reasons for seizure under Section 41 include no valid driving licence, no valid insurance, no valid roadworthiness certificate and no motor tax. Regulation 5 states the fees to be paid for release of a vehicle detained under Regulation 3. The fees are intended to cover the cost of detaining, moving and storing a seized vehicle, which are borne by An Garda Síochána. The fees are specified in Department of Transport regulations because the reasons for seizure are offences under the Road Traffic Acts, which fall under the remit of the Minister for Transport. However, the fees are determined by An Garda Síochána and the Department of Justice and are set on notification from the Minister for Justice to the Minister for Transport. Officials in my Department are engaged with counterparts in the Department of Justice with a review of these regulations and fees presently.

question: 1029. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation the length of time each of these 37 pieces has been unaccounted for, and whether any have been missing since prior to the migration to the new digital collection management system. [24315/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation I propose to take Questions Nos. 1027, 1028, 1029, 1030, 1031, 1032, 1033 and 1034 together. The State Art Collection (ISAC), which is managed by the Art Management Office in the Office of Public Works (OPW), is a unique cultural entity comprised of over 13500 artworks. The collection includes mainly 20th century Irish works of art as well as works acquired in more recent times, such as paintings, drawings, original prints, watercolours, sculpture, textiles, photographs in addition to multi-media works, music (composition and performances), poetry and applied art such as mosaics and art projects commissioned under the Per Cent for Art Scheme. Artworks are on display in over 500 client buildings across Ireland. The State Art Collection is a working collection being widely dispersed and mobile with over 80% of the artworks on display. The function of the collection differs from that of a gallery in that the State Art Collection is intended for public display in government offices and properties across Ireland. Artworks are displayed across a diverse range of internal and external spaces, in office buildings as well as older buildings with more traditional interiors; in garden and park settings, forecourts and courtyards. However, the presence of art in office environments and the public realm brings art into the everyday lives of people who visit and work in these spaces. By encouraging people to engage with contemporary art, it is the OPW’s intention to implement Government initiatives that support the arts in Ireland. When an artwork is acquired for the State Art Collection it is photographed and given a unique registration number before being placed on display in a client building. The artwork number and a label stating ‘Please Do Not Move Unless You Have The Prior Approval of the OPW’ are placed on the artwork in permanent ink. Details of the artwork are put into the collection management system. When an artwork is placed on loan to a client department, loan agreements are signed between the client borrowers and the OPW. The Art Management Office undertakes routine collection management audits of artworks for which it has responsibility in State buildings nationwide. These collection audits are conducted on a regular basis in line with the work programme and as part of the day-to-day management of the collection. In-person collection audits involve photographing, condition checking and documenting artworks on the collection management system. Digital audits are overseen remotely by the Art Management Office and undertaken by the client. Follow-up is carried out by the Art Management Office and all data is updated on the collection management system. There are several stages of collection management audits, all of which involve cooperation between the OPW and the client. Phase 2 of the 2025 audit process is currently ongoing and a more detailed analysis of matters arising will be included in the 2026 work programme. The second phase of the audit process is to make more detailed enquiries to follow up on matters arising from Phase 1. It would therefore be premature to release details into the public realm as the Collection Management team are still following up on these audit results. Phase 1 of the 2025 audits was completed in December 2025 and 2 of the artworks have since been located as part of the Phase 2 enquiries. Collection audits are part of the day to day collection management of the ISAC, which is a continuous process. In most cases where the location of artworks has changed in a client building, the artworks have been moved from their original documented location to another location within the building. Artworks may occasionally be moved by the client to facilitate renovation works, office moves etc. If such moves have not been notified to OPW when they take place, they can subsequently be documented through the audit and follow up processes. As the audit process progresses, the current locations of artworks are identified and records updated. At this point in time, as the 2025 audit process is still ongoing, it would be premature to contact An Garda Síochána in relation to thefts as there is currently no evidence that a theft has taken place. As outlined above, many artworks are located after the initial audit check in another part of the client building, or in another building related to the original location. It would also be premature to place information about the value of artworks audited in 2025 into the public realm, as the audit process is ongoing. However, as previously stated in the Irish Times article of 21st December 2025, the 37 artworks identified as unlocated in the 2025 audit programme range in value from €100 - €1150 with the majority being valued at under €500. The current policy for the OPW State Art Collection, which is in line with best practice and other national collections, is not to value artworks in the State Collection unless they are being placed on loan or exhibition with external third parties. The value of the State Art Collection is measured by its cultural and heritage significance not its financial value. An overall review of the State Art Collection policy documents is scheduled to take place in 2026. This review will include the ‘OPW State Art Collection: Collection Policy’ and ‘OPW State Art Collection: Information for Borrowers in Client Departments’. The latter policy states “ the Art Management Office will issue a Loan Agreement to be signed by Facilities Management/Corporate Services in the borrowing Department. It is the task of the borrower to take responsibility for the artworks placed on loan, their location and their condition, in line with Government directives in relation to asset management ” (pg. 9). Upon receiving a loan from the OPW State Art Collection, Facilities Management/Corporate Services in the client Department signs a loan agreement and takes joint responsibility for the safekeeping of the items on loan. The responsibility for the artworks on loan therefore lies primarily with the client department, while the OPW shares that responsibility in the form of conducting audits on the artworks which provide a level of accountability. In line with this responsibility, the 2026 works programme will involve an intensive audit programme and the focus will be on updating locations of artworks.

question: 1066. Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation for an update on his meeting with the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in relation to the repairs and re-opening of the Donegal town Courthouse; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [25667/26]
answer: Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation As the Deputy may be aware, under the provisions of the Courts Service Act 1998, management of the courts, including the provision of accommodation for court sittings, is the responsibility of the Courts Service which is independent in exercising its functions. The Minister understands that the Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Houses of the Oireachtas which may be of assistance to the Deputy regarding this matter: oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie.

question: 1100. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the number of non-nationals who are present in Ireland illegally without a work permit; the methods by which his Department or other relevant authorities seek to monitor this; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [23579/26]

1115. Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to provide clarification on the number of critical skills employment permits issued annually in the past four years and the number issued in the ICT, technology sector specifically; whether permit holders under this scheme may take up graduate or entry-level roles, or if the scheme is intended solely for more experienced positions; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24080/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment Ireland operates a managed employment permits system designed to address skills and labour shortages by regulating access to the Irish labour market through the Critical Skills Occupations List and the Ineligible Occupations List. Eligibility for a Critical Skills Employment Permit is determined by whether the occupation appears on the Critical Skills Occupations List and whether the role meets the required qualifications and remuneration criteria, rather than by sector alone, including the ICT and technology sector. As the scheme is specifically targeted at high-skill, high-demand professional roles, the positions eligible under the Critical Skills Employment Permit are generally not those typically regarded as graduate or entry level roles. However, those roles may still be eligible for a General Employment Permit, provided the application satisfies all other applicable criteria.
