question: 1132. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if the applications for the renewal of four work permits made by health care assistants based in the same nursing home (details supplied) can be granted; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24525/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment The four applications referenced by the Deputy currently remain on hold due to an ongoing Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) inspection of the employer. In accordance with standard procedure, applications linked to employers that are under WRC inspection are placed on hold pending the outcome of the review. Applicants seeking to renew their existing employment permit may continue to work while their renewal application is being processed. This ensures continuity for both employees and businesses. The applications will resume processing once the inspection has concluded and any necessary actions have been addressed To support applicants and employers, the Department has introduced a Self-Service Portal which provides real-time updates on employment permit application status. A dedicated mailbox for Oireachtas members is also available at tdepqueries@enterprise.gov.ie

question: 1144. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if a general employment permit renewal (details supplied) can be expedited; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24683/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment The Employment Permits Section of my Department continues to operate with a strong focus on efficiency and on improving overall processing timelines. The application for the renewal of the employment permit referenced was received on 27 February 2026. At present, the Employment Permits Section is processing renewal applications (across all renewable permit types) that were received up to 26 January 2026. Applications are assessed in the order in which they are received. Applicants who have submitted a valid application to renew an existing employment permit may continue to work while that application is being processed, including where the current permit has expired. This provision is intended to ensure continuity for both employees and employers. Current employment permit processing dates are published and updated regularly on my Department’s website. Where an employer considers that there are exceptional circumstances, they may request that an employment permit application be expedited by submitting a completed Employment Permit Expedite Request Form, accompanied by a detailed business case. The submission of a business case does not guarantee that an application will be expedited. To further support applicants and reduce the need for individual status queries, my Department has introduced a Self-Service Portal, which allows both employers and applicants to check the real-time status of their applications. In addition, a dedicated mailbox is available to Oireachtas members for employment permit-related queries at tdepqueries@enterprise.gov.ie.

question: 1159. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the timeframe for decision on an appeal (details supplied) in relation to an employment permit; and whether the decision can be expedited. [25890/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment The Employment Permits Act 2024 provides a statutory right of appeal where an employment permit application has been refused. Appeal applications are considered in accordance with the criteria set out in legislation, including those relating to remuneration and other eligibility requirements applicable to the permit type concerned. The appeal referenced by the Deputy has been received by the Department and is currently awaiting consideration. Appeals are processed in order of date of receipt. At present, the Department is examining appeals received on or around 18 November. While appeals are processed in date order, where an applicant considers that particular circumstances should be brought to the attention of the Department, they may submit a business case requesting that the appeal be expedited by contacting the Employment Permits Unit directly. Any such request is considered on a case-by-case basis and does not pre-empt the outcome of the appeal. The applicant and employer will be notified directly as soon as a decision has been reached.

question: 1186. Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment the number of work permits issued to persons from outside the UK and EEA intending to take up positions of dentists in the each of the years 2024, 2025 and to-date in 2026, in tabular form. [26662/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment Ireland operates a managed employment permits system designed to facilitate the admission of non-EEA and non-UK nationals to fill labour and skills shortages in the economy, while ensuring that opportunities continue to be available for Irish, EEA and UK nationals. The system is demand-led and employer-driven, with permits issued only where statutory criteria are met under the Employment Permits Act. Employment permits are issued for specific job roles with a named employer and are subject to salary thresholds, labour market needs, and, where applicable, sector-specific conditions. In the case of regulated professions, including dentistry, it is a requirement that permit holders must also comply with the relevant professional registration and regulatory requirements in order to lawfully take up employment in the State. The Employment Permits Section of the Department informs me that the table below shows the number of work permits issued to persons from outside the UK and EEA for the role of dentist from 2024 and to date in 2026. 2024 2025 2026 to date Dentist 45 72 15

question: 1514. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Education and Youth if a person (details supplied) will be facilitated to sit their State examinations; if she has discussed the matter with the Minister for Justice, Migration and Home Affairs, as it pertains to the individual concerned and more generally; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [26935/26]
answer: Minister for Education and Youth M atters relating to immigration are under the remit of my colleague Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Jim O’Callaghan. In relation to students undertaking a State Examination abroad, the State Examinations Commission (SEC) has advised that the only examination centre outside of Ireland is in Malta which facilitates Leaving Certificate candidates from the International School in Tripoli to take their examinations. Other than that, in limited circumstances the SEC facilitates a sitting of the Leaving Certificate abroad where a candidate has been selected to represent Ireland in a sporting or cultural competition or event and where that event clashes with some of their examinations. The SEC have advised that there are both cost and, more critically, very real security and integrity implications for facilitating a foreign sitting of a Leaving Certificate examinations and it is not an arrangement into which the SEC enters lightly when it does arise. In those cases the candidates involved are required to return to Ireland to complete their examinations once the event has finished. There may of course be other candidates who would wish to avail of such an arrangement if it was to be made available outside of the limited circumstances described. However, extending these limited arrangements to other students abroad would have serious logistical, security, integrity and cost considerations.

question: 1601. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport when it is envisaged that full telephone and broadband reception will be available at Dromid and Waterville; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [26372/26]
answer: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport I propose to take Questions Nos. 1601 and 1602 together. The National Broadband Plan (NBP) is the Government initiative to deliver high-speed broadband to all premises in Ireland. In addition, Ireland's Digital Connectivity Strategy published in December 2022, sets out a number of targets including that all Irish households and businesses will be covered by a Gigabit network no later than 2028. In County Kerry a significant investment of €107 million is being made under the NBP. There are 24,970 premises passed with a high-speed fibre broadband network and 25,785 premises available to order/pre-order, with over 7,150 premises now connected. A further circa 3,030 premises in Kerry will be passed by NBI’s high speed fibre broadband by the end of the network deployment. Dromid, Waterville is predominantly located in the AMBER area on the broadband map which is available on my Department’s website www.gov.ie/en/publication/5634d-national-broadband-plan-map/. NBI have advised that Dromid, falls within the Mastergeehy Electoral District of which 74 premises included in the NBP are now Ready for Service. A connection can be ordered from a number of broadband service providers. The list of available service providers can be found at nbi.ie/where-can-i-buy/. Premises in Balycleave village, which is under the Caragh Electoral District, includes 214 premises that will be served as part of the NBP. All premises are in Network Build in Progress stage and have an anticipated connection timeframe between July 2026 – December 2026. The latest information on when high-speed broadband will become available to the AMBER area can be found on National Broadband Ireland’s (NBI) website at nbi.ie/map/. This website is regularly updated providing the expected timeline for delivery and status of any works that are initiated at any point in time. NBI also has a dedicated email address, reps@nbi.ie, which can be used by Oireachtas members for specific queries. Along with the NBP intervention plan, progress is being made by commercial operators in expanding their next generation networks throughout the country including the deputy’s own county of Kerry ensuring the targets set out in the Digital Connectivity Strategy are achieved. These plans will see improved high speed broadband access across County Kerry. Phone service is primarily a matter for mobile network operators, operating on a commercial basis in a liberalised market, regulated by the Commission for Communications Regulation (ComReg). ComReg is statutorily independent in the exercise of its functions in accordance with Section 11 of the Communications Regulation Act 2002. The majority of Retail Service Providers offer a voice over IP phone service over the broadband network, ensuing that a phone service will become available. In addition, for mobile services, once broadband is active, Wi-Fi calling will improve mobile coverage within homes significantly. To assist consumers to choose the network provider that best meets their needs, ComReg continually updates and enhances its online national outdoor mobile coverage map (available at: coveragemap.comreg.ie) which provides information on mobile network operators’ outdoor coverage for 2G, 3G, 4G and 5G mobile networks.

question: 1677. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the position regarding housing supports for Ukrainian families that do not yet have permission to remain; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24402/26]
answer: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage I propose to take Questions Nos. 1677 and 1678 together. The Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration has the lead role in co-ordinating the Government wide response to Ukrainians fleeing the war. Ukrainian families arriving in Ireland as the result of the conflict in Ukraine are encouraged to register to receive their Temporary Protection Certificate (often called the yellow paper). This is overseen and administered by the Department of Justice and enables Ukrainian families to access necessary social welfare supports such as state provided accommodation. While my Department has no direct role in the provision of supports or the allocation of accommodation for Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection (BoTP’s), I have oversight of the “Offer a Home” scheme, in which property owners pledge their vacant homes to BoTP’s. This scheme is administered by the Local Authorities and BoTPs are entitled to avail of this scheme once they are in receipt of a Temporary Protection Certificate.

question: 1685. Deputy Rory Hearne asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his plans to increase preventions and exits from emergency accommodation for families who have been evicted; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24590/26]
answer: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage I propose to take Questions Nos. 1685 and 1686 together. My Department’s role in relation to homelessness involves the provision of a national framework of policy, legislation and funding to underpin the role of local authorities in addressing homelessness at local level. Statutory responsibility in relation to the provision of accommodation and related services for homeless persons rests with individual local authorities. Supporting individuals and families experiencing or at risk of experiencing homelessness is a priority for my Department and Government. Ireland signed the Lisbon Declaration in June 2021, which committed all signatories to work towards ending homelessness by 2030. I will continue to work with the National Homeless Action Committee to ensure an all of Government approach to drive the ambition of the Lisbon declaration. Critical to supporting households to exit homelessness is our continued investment in the social housing programme. Budget 2026 has continued the record level of investment in social housing, with €2.9bn in capital allocated to support the delivery of social homes by local authorities. This continued investment in the social housing programme will increase the supply of stock available to allocate to households on the social housing waiting list, including households in emergency accommodation. It is important that local authorities ensure that sufficient allocations are being made to families in emergency accommodation and a key focus for me is to reduce the time that families are spending in emergency accommodation. In September, I wrote to 21 local authorities that have families in emergency accommodation for more than 12 months and asked them to use all available housing schemes to exit these families from emergency accommodation. I have ring-fenced an additional €50 million, which I secured as part of the National Development Plan process, to exit households the longest in homeless accommodation with a focus in the first instance on larger families with children and Housing First clients. This funding is in addition to the €325 million already committed to the Social Housing Second-Hand Acquisitions Programme in 2025. Our new housing plan, ‘ Delivering Homes, Building Communities: An Action Plan on Housing Supply and Targeting Homelessness’ is an integrated housing and homelessness plan. The new plan is based on two key pillars: activating the supply of 300,000 more homes; and supporting people to have a home of their own. Increased supply is key to addressing homelessness. Government is focused on making sure that everyone has access to good quality, affordable and secure homes that suit their needs. Over €9 billion in capital funding will be made available for housing in 2026. Our new Plan recognises that homelessness is the single most pressing social issue that we face and introduces a number of key measures to address homelessness. Prevention of homelessness in the first instance is an absolute priority. There are many preventions initiatives already underway in my own Department and across Government. This includes the provision of social and affordable housing, HAP and homeless HAP, and our strong tenancy protection legislation. In order to ensure a fully aligned all-of-Government approach under the Plan, we are committing to develop a national Homelessness Prevention Framework within which homelessness can be prevented in a structured and planned way with tailored prevention measures for each potential at risk cohort. This Framework will be in place in 2026. Addressing family homelessness is another key priority for Government. Our new housing plan commits to the development of a Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan. This will bring together key stakeholders to drive the continued focus on preventing children and families entering emergency accommodation, providing enhanced supports for children experiencing homelessness, as well as measures to accelerate exits and reduce the time spent by children and their families in homeless emergency accommodation. Consultations with key stakeholders are currently underway and it is anticipated that the Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan will be published by end of Q2 2026. Ensuring that individuals and families experiencing homelessness are provided with accommodation and supports is critical. Budget 2026 provides a total allocation of €563.5m to address homelessness. This includes €513.5m in current funding to ensure local authorities can provide sufficient emergency accommodation as well as essential related services including homelessness prevention supports, day services, and tenancy sustainment measures. Additionally, €50 million in capital funding will allow local authorities to invest in the provision of local authority or NGO owned emergency accommodation facilities, developing a more sustainable approach to the delivery of emergency accommodation and ensuring that services are tailored for the needs of clients. Our new Housing Plan also provides dedicated capital funding of €100 million which will be ring-fenced to support local authorities to acquire properties to tackle long-term homelessness. It will be used specifically to acquire suitable units to exit families the longest in emergency accommodation and for Housing First, units for individuals with complex needs experiencing homelessness.

question: 1710. Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the specific measures he is taking to provide accommodation for one-parent families given the higher vulnerability of this group to experience homelessness; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24974/26]
answer: Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage I propose to take Questions Nos. 1664, 1665 and 1710 together. The Government is acutely aware of the housing challenges faced by many sectors of society. It is for that reason that Ireland’s new housing plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025-2030, published on 13 November 2025, is based on two pillars: activating supply and supporting people. Delivering Homes, Building Communities recognises that homelessness is the single most pressing social issue that affects individuals and families in Ireland right now. Increasing housing supply is key to addressing homelessness. Over the lifetime of the new housing plan, a minimum of 300,000 new homes of all types will be delivered across the country, including 72,000 new social homes and 90,000 affordable housing supports to assist people to buy or rent at a cost they can sustain. The prevention of homelessness in the first instance is essential. There are many prevention initiatives already underway, including the provision of social and affordable housing, HAP and homeless HAP, and our strong tenancy protection legislation. To ensure a fully aligned all-of-Government approach, the Government is committed under the new housing plan to developing a national Homelessness Prevention Framework within which homelessness can be prevented in a structured and planned way with tailored prevention measures for each potential at risk cohort. This Framework will be in place in 2026. Addressing family homelessness is a particular priority for the Government and, in that regard, Delivering Homes, Building Communities commits to the development of a Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan. This will bring together key stakeholders to drive a continued focus on preventing children and families entering emergency accommodation, providing enhanced supports for children experiencing homelessness, as well as measures to accelerate exits and reduce the time spent by children and their families in homeless emergency accommodation. It is anticipated that the Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan will be in place by end of Q2 2026. The Government is also establishing a more robust legal and policy framework to support increased investment in the rental market to increase supply and choice for renters and, over time, reduce market rents. The Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 came into operation on 1 March 2026, introducing a new national rent control for all tenancies, which limits rent increases to inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) up to a maximum of 2%. For new build apartments and student-specific accommodation, however, rent increases are capped at the level of inflation (CPI) only. The Act provides significant improvements in security of tenure for renters. A tenant moving into a dwelling on or after 1 March 2026 will have certainty that while they remain in the tenancy their rent can only increase by inflation, up to a maximum of 2%, in all tenancies other than new apartments or Student Specific Accommodation for the following six years. Rent increases in tenancies that began before 1 March 2026 will be restricted to inflation, up to a maximum of 2%. In addition, the following affordable housing supports are open and available to all applicants who meet the relevant criteria, including single parent households: • Local Authority Affordable Purchase Scheme • First Home Scheme • Local Authority Home Loan • Local Authority Purchase and Renovation Loan • Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant • Help to Buy A number of these schemes can be combined, thereby providing additional affordability support. Further information is available here: Doors Open Campaign

question: 1871. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Social Protection for an update on the commitment to abolish the means test for carers; the timeline envisaged for any such reform; the interim measures being considered in light of the financial pressures currently facing carers and their families; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24898/26]
answer: Minister for Social Protection The Carer’s Allowance is the main scheme by which my department provides income support to carers. Expenditure on Carer’s Allowance in 2026 is estimated to exceed €1.4 billion. At the end of March there were more than 106,000 carers receiving this payment. The Programme for Government has set out a timeline which commits to significantly increasing the income disregards for Carer’s Allowance in each Budget, with a view to phasing out the means test during the lifetime of this Government. This process is already underway. Last July the amount of weekly earnings disregarded was increased to €625 for a single person and €1,250 for a couple. As part of Budget 2026, I announced further changes to the Carer’s Allowance means test that will be introduced in July. The weekly income disregard will increase from €625 to €1,000 for a single person, and from €1,250 to €2,000 for carers who are part of couple. Since June 2022, there have been cumulative increases to the disregards of over 200%. The single carer disregard has increased by €667.50 and the couple disregard by €1,335. These are significant increases. The reforms in July will see more carers qualify for Carer’s Allowance. For example, a carer in a two-adult household with an income of approximately €110,000 will retain their full Carer’s Allowance payment and even with an income of €138,000 will retain a partial payment. The recent improvements outlined are evidence of the Government’s determination to deliver on its commitment to phase out the Carer's Allowance means test over the lifetime of the Government. We will continue to progress this commitment in light of the prevailing budgetary conditions. The government is keenly aware that many people and families, including carers and their families, are facing higher energy costs at the moment as a result of the conflict in the Middle East. For this reason, we announced a €250 million energy relief package last month for households and businesses. As part of this package, the Fuel Allowance season will be extended by an additional four weeks. This targeted measure provides practical assistance and means that the 470,000 households in receipt of the Fuel Allowance, which include many carers and disabled people, will receive additional financial support of €38 per week until May 1st, totalling €152. For anyone who needs immediate assistance, the Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme is available. Under the scheme, my department may make Additional Needs Payments to help meet essential expenses that a person cannot pay from their weekly income or other personal and household resources. These payments are available through our Community Welfare Officers. The payment is available to anyone who needs it and qualifies, whether the person is currently receiving a social welfare payment or working on a low income. Furthermore, under the scheme, a Heating Supplement may be paid to assist people with exceptional heating costs due to ill health, infirmity or a medical condition and are unable to meet those costs out of household income. Heating Supplement is not restricted to the fuel season and can be paid throughout the full year. Any person who considers that they may have an entitlement to an Additional Needs Payment or a Heating Supplement is encouraged to contact their local community welfare service. There is a National Community Welfare Contact Centre in place - 0818-607080 - which will direct callers to the appropriate office. In addition, applications for Additional Needs Payments can be made online via www.mywelfare.ie. I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question: 1943. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 217 of 24 March 2026, if he will address concerns raised in correspondence (details supplied) with specific focus on the fact that this is no longer a question of legal process, but one of enforcement failure and accountability; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [26418/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As the Deputy will be aware, I am unable to comment on the details of individual cases or intervene in private, civil or international legal matters which are the subject of court proceedings either in Ireland or another jurisdiction. The procedures for dealing with situations of international parental child abduction involving countries which are party to the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction are set out in the Child Abduction and Enforcements of Custody Orders Act 1991. EC Regulation 2019/1111 (Brussels IIb) supplements and supports the terms of the Hague Convention in instances of international parental child abduction between Member States, excluding Denmark. By way of information, regarding the cooperation between the Irish Central Authority and relevant authorities, the Irish Central Authority acts as a transmitting and receiving agency, communicating any updates or requests for information between an applicant and the authorities of the other state. Any administrative and judicial measures required to decide on the return of a child are taken by the authorities in the contracting state that the child has been taken to. The Irish Central Authority is not involved in the legal proceedings of the other country. It relies on the authorities of the other state to progress the application through their institutions and to keep it informed of any developments or advise it of any information required from the applicant. The Hague Convention, which Poland and Ireland are signatory to, specifically mandates that all return proceedings are handled by the authorities of the signatory country that a child has been taken to. The Irish Central Authority is unable to influence how each country structures the required proceedings.

question: 1944. Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the action being taken by his Department to improve the processing timeline of long stay D join family visa applications; if consideration would be given to the allocation of additional staff to deal with these application and reduce current timelines; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [27355/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1945, 1944, 1946, 2170 and 2173 together. I can advise the Deputy that my Department currently operates seven overseas Visa Offices in addition to the Visa Office in Dublin. These are located in Abuja, Beijing, London, Moscow, Ankara, Abu Dhabi and New Delhi. In addition, staff of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade process certain visa applications in Irish Embassies abroad under delegated authority from my Department. While processing times can vary across the different Visa Offices and Irish Embassies, the majority of visas are processed within stated target times. In respect of join family visa applications, the majority receive a first instance decision within the 12 month business target. Processing times and decisions at the Dublin Visa Office and the Overseas Visa Offices can be checked at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions It should be noted that some applications can take considerably longer. Processing times for all applications are influenced by a number of factors. The time it can take varies depending on the type and complexity of application; individual circumstances; peak application periods; such as holidays or the start of the school year; and, crucially, the quality and completeness of the application lodged. Verifying an application is an important part of our immigration system and the checks involved can take time to complete. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants, and I want to assure anyone who has made an application for a visa that my Department is doing everything possible to progress these applications as quickly as possible. Ireland remains firmly committed to upholding its obligations under the European Convention of Human Rights, including the right to respect for family life under Article 8. In line with the established jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights, a balance must be struck between facilitating family reunification and the State's responsiblity to maintain an effective immigration system. In this context, the ongoing Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) modernisation programme is designed to support a more efficient, transparent and accessible immigration system. The recent establishment of dedicated teams for Application Submission and Join Family Case Processing are intended to help streamline workflows, reduce duplication and strengthen expertise, thereby improving the service delivery for join family visa applications. question: 1947. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the rollout of Operation Encompass; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [23585/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Programme for Government commits to "fully implement the Zero Tolerance: Third National Strategy on Domestic, Sexual, Gender Based Violence Zero Tolerance (DSGBV) 2022-2026". Action 2.5.4 of the Zero Tolerance Implementation Plan 2025-2026 is "to scope and develop an operational framework to introduce Operation Encompass in the Irish system, including identifying any necessary legislative changes and consulting with relevant stakeholders" and work to achieve this is being progressed. As the Deputy may be aware, the General Scheme of the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences, Domestic Violence and International Instruments) Bill 2025, which includes a provision to allow Gardaí to inform a designated person in a school that a domestic violence incident has occurred in a pupil’s home, was approved by Government on 21 October 2025. Pre-legislative scrutiny of the General Scheme took place on 20 January. An Operation Encompass pilot in Drogheda is scheduled to commence in September 2026 and run to September 2027 during which time it will be subject to ongoing monitoring and evaluation. The pilot represents the first implementation of Operation Encompass in this jurisdiction and is being progressed on a phased and voluntary basis. Primary and post-primary schools in the Drogheda area have been invited to express interest, with initial rollout focused on those schools that opt in and are supported to participate. The participating schools will be – as far as possible - within the Drogheda Garda Station District to allow for close interaction between the local Gardaí and designated persons at each school. This approach allows for testing of processes, safeguarding protocols, and operational arrangements before any wider rollout. I was pleased to attend a learning event focused on the Drogheda pilot, held on 19 March in Drogheda, and bringing together An Garda Síochána, the PSNI, schools, education partners and government officials from the North and South to exchange information and lessons learned from rolling out Operation Encompass across Northern Ireland. This marked the commencement of a structured engagement and learning phase designed to build out the operational, governance, and safeguarding structures required to support the implementation of the pilot.

question: 1948. Deputy Seán Crowe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he is aware of significant delays in the processing of Stamp 1G applications; the average wating time to receive approval of a Stamp 1G application; his Department’s target time to approve an application; the number of applications being processed; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [23586/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I understand that the Deputy has clarified that he is referring to applicants seeking an extension of their Stamp 1G permission who have submitted a valid, in-time Extension of Student Conditions (ESTC) application to my Department, having reached the maximum time permitted under the Third Level Graduate Programme. An application for an ESTC is intended for unforeseen or unusual circumstances. It is not intended for students or graduates who fail to secure an employment permit and who have exhausted the maximum time permitted under the Third Level Graduate Programme. Each ESTC application is considered on its own individual merits taking into account any exceptional circumstances put forward by the applicant. Where such permissions are extended it is generally for a period not exceeding 6 months. To be fair to all applicants, applications are dealt with in chronological order by date received. My Department endeavours to process applications as quickly as possible. However, processing times may vary due to a number of factors, such as the number of applications on hand, individual circumstances, the complexity of applications, whether further information is required, and the resources available. My Department are currently processing ESTC applications received from October 2025, and there are approximately a total of 2,700 applications on hand. There has been a significant increase in recent months in ESTC applications and these are being dealt with as expeditiously as possible. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at:portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ The below table details the number of ESTC applications received from 2021 to 2025. 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 ESTC Received 1778 2498 3045 3591 5372 *Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing.

question: 1949. Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the actions his Department is taking to address anti-social behaviour in Dublin; and to prevent racist attacks and ensure the better protection for our migrant communities; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [23668/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Government is taking a range of measure to tackle antisocial behaviour and public safety, including; • Budget 2026 provides unprecedented funding of €2.74 billion for An Garda Síochána to support recruitment and staffing. • Introducing Community Safety Partnerships around the country, to develop Community Safety Plans that are tailored for every area. • The deployment of body-worn cameras for Gardaí in Dublin, Waterford and Limerick on a pilot basis with nationwide rollout to follow. • Continued expansion of youth justice and youth diversion measures to reduce youth offending and improve safety for everyone in the community. A number of actions are also contained in the Programme for Government to reduce instances of anti-social behaviour. These include a commitment to enact legislation to combat anti-social behaviour through enhanced use of Anti-Social Behaviour Warnings and Anti-Social Behaviour Orders. Work to progress these commitments has commenced. The Government is determined to tackle hate-motivated crime and protect vulnerable communities. The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 strengthens the law by ensuring perpetrators face tougher penalties where hatred is proven to be a motivating factor, or where hatred is demonstrated based on the identity of the victim. Legislation has been complemented by active stakeholder engagement to inform a new Migration and Integration Strategy, due to be published this year. This Programme for Government commitment outlines how we intend to meet the demands and the opportunities facing our society and economy over the next decade. Anti-racism and integration funds support initiatives nationwide promoting inclusion and combatting prejudice. Grants to a value of €3.9 million awarded to 94 projects across Ireland under the Ireland Against Racism Fund since the fund launched in 2023. The National Action Plan Against Racism (NAPAR) 2023 -2027, a state led, co-ordinated approach to combatting racism is being implemented. It is intended that the actions will have a significant positive impact on all minority ethnic communities and faith-based groups in Ireland. The second NAPAR Implementation report for 2024 was recently published on the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration’s website. In Q4 2025, officials from the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration held meetings with a wide range of other Government Departments and public sector bodies on a bilateral basis to discuss overall progress on the implementation of their relevant actions under NAPAR for 2025, along with their key challenges, opportunities, and next steps. An Garda Síochána takes hate crime very seriously. Every hate crime reported to An Garda Síochána is professionally investigated, and victims are supported during the criminal justice process. I would encourage anyone that has experienced incidents to report these to An Garda Síochána. An Garda Síochána also continues in its efforts to strengthen its network of diversity officers to support victims and those affected by hate discrimination in communities around the country. There is an extensive network of trained Garda Diversity Officers in place nationwide to provide reassurance, build trust, and address concerns. Gardaí are also actively engaged with advocacy groups to support minority and diverse communities.

question: 1954. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he has considered the recommendations of the Law Reform Commission’s 2026 report on compensating victims of crime; the Government’s position on the report; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [23784/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1954, 1955, 1956, 1957, 1958, 1972, 1973, 1974, 1975, 1976 and 1977 together. I welcome the recent publication of the Law Reform Commission’s Report on Compensating Victims of Crime. The Commission has produced a very thorough and expert examination of a complex issue. Existing arrangements for compensating victims of crime have remained largely unchanged for over 50 years and are in need of reform. Recognising this, the Programme for Government committed to placing the Criminal Injuries Compensation Tribunal on a statutory footing. Work on the drafting of the necessary legislation will now be prioritised, taking account of the recommendations contained in the LRC report. Other reforms of the existing scheme are also being progressed. The Deputy will be aware that in 2021, the then Government agreed to introduce a revised Scheme and a number of immediate reforms were introduced. This was acknowledged as a first step towards improving the operation of the Scheme. To support this, an inter-departmental working group chaired by my Department examined many of the issues relevant to longer-term reform, including the possibility of introducing compensation for pain and suffering. I have been advised that this inter-departmental group will reconvene shortly. The recommendations of the Law Reform Commission’s Report on Compensating Victims of Crime will be of great assistance in the further development of these proposals for reform and I look forward to receiving an update in due course. In relation to funding of the Scheme, as part of the annual estimates process, the Scheme is provided with a yearly allocation as part of my Department’s overall budget. In circumstances where the original allocation provided for the Scheme is less than the total expenditure on awards made by the Criminal Injuries Compensation Tribunal, additional monies may be secured by way of supplementary provision being made available to the Scheme. In the meantime, I can assure the Deputy that applications continue to be processed by the Criminal Injuries Compensation Tribunal Secretariat as far as practicable, pending Government agreement on amendments to the existing Scheme. I am advised that the Secretariat provides updates and responds to queries from applicants on the progress of their applications. Separately, I am committed to ensuring the process for financial support for victims of violent crime remains open to victims while the longer-term reforms are progressed. I intend to bring forward proposals to Government shortly to amend the existing Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme to reflect the recent judgment of the Court of Justice of the European Union.

question: 1959. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons with a valid deportation order signed that are still in Ireland; the number currently still in State provided accommodation; and the reason they are being provided with accommodation when they no longer have any entitlement to be in Ireland. [23797/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules based. The enforcement aspects of our laws, including deportation orders, are an essential requirement for the system to work effectively and to ensure that there is confidence in the application of our legislation in this area. Deportations are costly and complex to enforce. It is the preferred option to return people voluntarily and my Department has a voluntary return programme to assist people to return before a deportation order is issued. If a person does not remove themselves from the State following the issuance of a deportation order, they will be removed, and my Department has taken action to significantly improve immigration enforcement measures and increase removals. The number of deportation orders signed in 2024 (2,403) increased by 180% compared to 2023 (857). In 2025, 4,700 deportation orders were signed, an increase of 96% compared to 2024. In 2024, 1,122 people departed from the State under various mechanisms (i.e. enforced deportation, voluntary return etc.). In 2025, 2,111 people had their departure confirmed through these pathways, an increase of 88% compared to 2024. In 2025, six charter flight operations removed 205 people from the State. Of these, five operations to non-EU destinations removed 182 people who were subject to deportation orders and one operation removed 23 EU citizens on grounds of criminality. Two charter operations to date in 2026 have seen the removal of 96 people from the State, including 33 EU citizens who were removed on grounds of criminality. Further charter operations will be conducted throughout the year. The enforcement of deportation orders is an operational matter for the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB), and my Department works closely with the GNIB to progress arrangements for the removal of people subject to deportation orders. If a person issued with a deportation order does not leave the State independently then they are required to present to the GNIB in accordance with the conditions of their deportation order. As Ireland does not operate routine exit checks at Irish borders, it is not possible to confirm in all instances that a person has departed the State. A person is only recorded as being deported when their deportation has been enforced by An Garda Síochána or when officials have been provided with evidence that they have left Ireland. While over 300 of the people subject to deportation orders above have confirmed they have left the State independently since 2020, it is the case that a significantly larger number of individuals who were subject to Deportation orders have left the State without notifying the relevant authorities. I am informed that the Garda National Immigration Bureau has reviewed a large sample of cases of people subject to deportation orders; their inquiries suggest a very significant number of these individuals have left the State. The number of people resident in the International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres who have been refused permission to remain in the State is a small proportion of the total IPAS resident group of over 33,000 people. Currently, there are approximately 650 people subject to deportation orders residing in IPAS accommodation. This number fluctuates regularly as people leave Ireland under the relevant return pathways, and as new orders are made. Some people subject to deportation orders may have the enforcement of their order suspended due to legal proceedings or due to personal circumstances such as health grounds. Others will be in the process of arranging to leave the State as outlined above. The tables below detail the number of deportation orders signed, as well as the number enforced, from 2021 to 2025. question: 1963. Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the role that a service (details supplied) has in processing visa applications in the Irish Embassy in India; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [23905/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that in recent years my Department has taken a number of steps to upgrade the visa processing system and improve the service offered to individuals applying for Irish visas. This has included availing of services provided by VFS Global at their Visa Application Centres (VACs). VFS Global provides administrative and logistical support services. It does not have any role in the decision-making process, which is the sole remit of officials from my Department, as is the case in India, or the Department of Foreign Affairs in other parts of the world. Applications for Irish visas made by residents of India are submitted at VACs located in Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Chandigarh, Chennai, Cochin, Hyderabad, Jalandhar, Kolkata, Mumbai, New Delhi and Pune. I had the opportunity to visit the VAC in New Delhi earlier this year where I met with senior staff members and had a tour of the building in which they provide their services. A number of services are provided for the fee charged by VFS, including the initial administration of applications and transmitting documents between customers and the Visa Office. Additionally, VFS Global offers a number of optional services, the fees for which are detailed on their website, at the following address: visa.vfsglobal.com/ind/en/irl/additional-services I can advise the Deputy that my Department makes no payments to VFS Global for their services. When a person in India applies for an Irish visa they pay a service fee to VFS Global directly for their services. The use of VFS Global’s services provides greater accessibility to customers across a wider geographical area, particularly in large countries or countries where Ireland does not have consular representation. The use of VFS Global’s centres reduces courier and travel costs for customers whose nearest Irish Visa Office or Embassy could be located thousands of kilometres away. I can advise the Deputy the fees applied by VFS Global are in addition to the application fees for Irish visas. The fees for Irish visas are, €60 for an single entry visas, €100 for a multi entry visas and €25 for a transit visa. Further information regarding Irish visa fees and exemptions are available at the following address: www.irishimmigration.ie/preclearance-and-entry-visas-fees/

question: 1964. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether he has been personally briefed on the findings or recommendations arising from the Internal Audit Unit’s examination of attendance management practices, including the exchange-of-duty system. [23951/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1964 and 1965 together. The IPS is responsible for the day-to-day running and operations of the prisons. I am advised that the Irish Prison Service HR Directorate have introduced a number of measures in recent years to both monitor and enhance attendance arrangements at a prison level. These include: • Exchange of Duty compliance levels at each prison now form part of the annual deliverables for each Prison Governor; • The processes and procedures in place in relation to Exchange of Duty are managed under ongoing review and updated regularly to ensure compliance & accountability. The most recent update came into effect at the beginning of 2026. • The introduction of HR Directorate annual compliance reviews of prisons with the Exchange of Duty system; • Updating the current Time & Attendance System. The existing system is not user friendly and requires manual interventions to develop reports necessary to support prisons in monitoring levels of compliance; and • The completion of a procurement process to install a system which will deliver enhanced monitoring and automatic restrictions for individual participation with the Exchange of Duty process, based on set parameters. This new time & attendance system will be operational mid-2027. My Department’s Internal Audit Unit has conducted audits across all of the prisons and they have examined attendance management in their work. A number of recommendations on attendance management practices, including the exchange of duty process, are being implemented.

question: 1967. Deputy Rory Hearne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the assistance that his Department provide to Iranian academics who have been accepted by Irish universities or hold valid hosting agreements for research positions in Ireland, and are awaiting visa processing before they can travel safely to Ireland; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24000/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I appreciate that those who have been granted scholarships or hosting agreements by Higher Level Institutions in Ireland are eager to take up their positions. I can assure the Deputy that, while processing times can vary across the different Visa Offices and Irish Embassies, the majority of visas are processed within stated target times. However, some applications can take considerably longer. Processing times for all applications are influenced by a number of factors, including the type and complexity of application, individual circumstances, peak application periods such as holidays or the start of the school year, and the quality and completeness of the application lodged. Visa applications can only be determined when all the required information is received and considered by the Visa Office. This assessment is not limited to the documentation submitted by the applicant. The Visa Office also must take steps to verify the details and/or documentation submitted in support of the application. These requirements are detailed in the privacy notice which all visa applicants agree to upon submitting their application. Visa and preclearance applications provide legal avenues for people moving to Ireland. It is important to recall these applications are screening processes, designed to establish that the person has a legitimate reason to come to Ireland prior to travel. Verifying an application is an important part of our immigration system and the checks involved can take time to complete.

question: 1968. Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to clarify the current legal position in Ireland regarding the retail sale of products containing sulphuric acid above 15% concentration; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24014/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Sulphuric acid at concentrations above 15% is listed as a Restricted Explosive Precursor as per Annex I of the Regulation (EU) 2019/1148 on Marketing and Use of Explosives Precursors, and therefore may only be made available to Professional Users/Economic Operators. Article 5(3) further states: “A Member State may maintain or establish a licensing regime allowing certain restricted explosives precursors to be made available to, or to be introduced, possessed or used by members of the general public at concentrations not higher than the corresponding upper limit values set out in column 3 of the table in Annex I.” No licensing regime was provided for by the State upon the publishing of S.I. 66 of 2026, the European Union (Marketing and Use of Explosives Precursors) Regulations 2026. Therefore, Restricted Explosives Precursors shall not be made available to, or introduced, possessed or used by members of the general public.

question: 1969. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if an opportunity will be given to solicitors to provide feedback on his proposed plan to simplify the criminal legal aid payment in the District Courts; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24016/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1969 and 2066 together. The Government recognises the crucial role played by the legal professions in the effective administration of criminal justice. It is important to note that the Programme for Government contains three commitments in relation to Criminal Legal Aid. The first is to reform the operation of the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme. The second is to restore criminal legal aid fees, and the third is to enact the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Bill. It is my intention to fulfil all three commitments. It is proposed from 1 July 2026 to pay a set fee for representation from the beginning to the end of a case, removing the link between payments and the number of appearances, or legal aid certificates granted. This proposal is informed by a review carried out my Department, of 350,000 District Court Cases which took place between 2022 and 2023. The proposed reform aims to address structural issues identified during this review, such as additional adjournments resulting from the payment per appearance model and to speed up case resolution. The fee would be payable regardless of number of appearances, if there are multiple certificates for cases heard together, or number of accused represented. The proposal fulfils the Programme for Government commitment to reform criminal legal aid and fully restore fees. My Department has been engaging extensively with relevant stakeholders, including An Garda Síochána, the Probation Service and Courts Service on the review and proposed changes to the scheme. Officials from my Department also met with the Bar Council and Law Society together in May, July and October 2025, and both bodies were invited to make submissions on the findings of the review by November 2025. An initial submission from the Law Society was received on 14 November 2025, the details of which were considered before the report was finalised. Correspondence was also received from the Bar Council. I can assure the Deputy that my officials have had ongoing engagement with the professional bodies and most recently met with the Law Society and the Bar Council in early March. Further submissions have been received from the Law Society and from the Bar Council on the 27 March and 2 April respectively. My Department is currently considering the content of these submissions and will continue to engage with the Law Society and Bar Council in advance of the introduction of the new arrangements on 1 July.

Work on the drafting of the necessary legislation will now be prioritised, taking account of the recommendations contained in the LRC report. Other reforms of the existing scheme are also being progressed. The Deputy will be aware that in 2021, the then Government agreed to introduce a revised Scheme and a number of immediate reforms were introduced. This was acknowledged as a first step towards improving the operation of the Scheme. To support this, an inter-departmental working group chaired by my Department examined many of the issues relevant to longer-term reform, including the possibility of introducing compensation for pain and suffering. I have been advised that this inter-departmental group will reconvene shortly. The recommendations of the Law Reform Commission’s Report on Compensating Victims of Crime will be of great assistance in the further development of these proposals for reform and I look forward to receiving an update in due course. In relation to funding of the Scheme, as part of the annual estimates process, the Scheme is provided with a yearly allocation as part of my Department’s overall budget. In circumstances where the original allocation provided for the Scheme is less than the total expenditure on awards made by the Criminal Injuries Compensation Tribunal, additional monies may be secured by way of supplementary provision being made available to the Scheme. In the meantime, I can assure the Deputy that applications continue to be processed by the Criminal Injuries Compensation Tribunal Secretariat as far as practicable, pending Government agreement on amendments to the existing Scheme. I am advised that the Secretariat provides updates and responds to queries from applicants on the progress of their applications. Separately, I am committed to ensuring the process for financial support for victims of violent crime remains open to victims while the longer-term reforms are progressed. I intend to bring forward proposals to Government shortly to amend the existing Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme to reflect the recent judgment of the Court of Justice of the European Union.

question: 1978. Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if a family (details supplied) can be provided with alternate accommodation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24074/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1978 and 1979 together. The Department cannot provide information on individual cases, but my officials, including the IPAS Resident Welfare Team, are aware of this family’s needs and have engaged with them. I can assure the Deputy that IPAS has a number of protocols and procedures in place for considering applications for transfer in cases of medical priority, where people are undergoing specialist treatment or may need to live within a reasonable travelling distance to a hospital. Individuals and families request transfers for a variety of reasons and IPAS facilitates those requests as appropriate and where possible. Transfers can be more difficult in complex cases, and also in the context of limited available accommodation options. Transfers are dependent on accommodation availability, particularly in instances where a resident has specific personal, health, and accessibility needs. IPAS also has guidelines in place which were developed in conjunction with the Department of Social Protection and the HSE for transport to medical appointments and medical services for residents.

question: 1982. Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether a proposal by his Department (details supplied) to prevent those who have accessed social protection payments within the past two years from applying for citizenship applies to non-refugee applicants for citizenship; which social protection payments are included; and the current status of the proposal. [24113/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Last November, Minister O'Callaghan and I secured Government approval to introduce new policies and legislative changes to strengthen Ireland’s migration and asylum system to ensure it is rules-based, efficient and more aligned with EU Member States. As part of this, we intend to make a number of changes to the rules on the granting of Irish citizenship. One proposed change relates to the introduction of a new statutory naturalisation condition requiring applicants to be self-sufficient. Being self-sufficient will mean that the applicant should not be indebted to the State or be in receipt of certain social protection payments during a defined period prior to submitting an application. It is not the intention to prevent anybody who has ever received a welfare payment from applying for citizenship. There will be certain payments that will not affect a person’s ability to apply and be granted citizenship. The outlined conditions relating to self-sufficiency will require amendments to the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956 via the regular parliamentary process, following consultation with other relevant Departments.

question: 1983. Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will meet the families of those bereaved and injured by the Omagh bombing. [24126/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The bombing in the town of Omagh on the 15 August 1998 was the single worst atrocity of the Troubles. The Government has recognised the terrible toll that the bombing took on so many and has made clear its commitment to doing everything possible to assist the UK Omagh Bombing Inquiry in its work. In addition to the measures already implemented to support the disclosure of Irish State materials to the Inquiry, I have brought forward legislation to enable the taking of oral testimony in this jurisdiction. That Bill, the International Co-operation (Omagh Bombing Inquiry) Bill, is due to be considered by the Select Committee on Justice, Home Affairs and Migration today and I hope, with the support of both Houses, that it will be enacted before the Summer. As regards whether I will meet the Omagh families, I am always open to considering requests for meetings. There has been a long history of engagement between the families and Government representatives. Last June, senior officials from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade organised a meeting with the families of victims, survivors and legal representatives following the hearing of opening statements by core participants to the Inquiry. Some 40 people attended. The meeting provided an opportunity to hear the concerns of those present and to answer any questions that they had in relation to the form assistance by Irish authorities would take. Since then a number of the families have initiated legal proceedings against the State seeking the establishment of a parallel inquiry in this jurisdiction. Those proceedings are ongoing and obviously impose some limitations on what could be discussed with families at any meeting. Apart from the constraints arising from those live legal proceedings, I am conscious that there is a statutory inquiry underway in Northern Ireland. It is my view that matters that touch on the Inquiry's remit and operation are primarily a matter of communication between the Inquiry itself and the families, many of whom have the formal status of core participants before the Inquiry. It is for the Inquiry, within its own rules, to determine what information to share with core participants including in relation to co-operation with this jurisdiction. The Deputy will be aware that Counsel to the Inquiry at its hearing on 19 March comprehensively addressed the operation of the Memorandum of Understanding that is in place between the Government and the Chairman of the Inquiry and noted the considerable efforts that have been made by Irish authorities and the effective progress being made to respond to its requests. I understand the Inquiry also referred at its hearing to its engagement with my officials in relation to the General Scheme of the Bill which I shared with them last December. As I have said I am open to considering all requests for meetings but would wish to avoid any misunderstanding as to the scope of the matters that might be discussed.

question: 1985. Deputy Louise O'Reilly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of staff that have been allocated to each Dublin metropolitan region; the number of these posts that have been filled; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24173/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the allocation and deployment of Garda resources throughout the state. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Garda personnel nationally, including a breakdown of Garda Staff assigned by division and station from 2010 to the end of February 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. This can be found at the following links: 2010-2025 www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/garda-strength-breakdown-2025.html 2026www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/february-2026.html Under Budget 2026, I secured record funding of €2.74 billion for An Garda Síochána to support recruitment and staffing. An Garda Síochána have partnered with Staffline to recruit Garda Staff, with a number of open Garda Staff competitions currently running. Details are available at: www.garda.ie/en/careers/career-opportunities-for-garda-staff/ As of the end of February 2026, the latest date for when figures are available, there were 3,679 Garda Staff within An Garda Síochána, accounting for about 19% of the overall Garda workforce, This represents an increase of over 75% since 2015 when there were approximately 2,000 Garda Staff. Garda Staff are an integral part of our policing service and they are involved in the provision of a wide range of administrative, professional and technical services. As well as providing clerical support and financial management functions in Garda stations and offices across the country Garda Staff also carry out a range of specialised support roles. The significant increase in Garda Staff has enabled 900 Gardaí to be freed up for frontline duties.

question: 1986. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of complaints made to Fiosrú’s new unit for tackling complaints against members relating to domestic and sexual abuse; the frequency with which he is seeking updates on measures to address culture in An Garda Síochána; his views on the Programme for Government commitments to ensure transparency and exchange of accurate information designed to improve culture across the security and policing services generally; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [23191/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Under the Policing, Security and Community Safety (PSCS) Act 2024, Fiosrú is an independent body with statutory objectives and aims to enhance the oversight and accountability of policing in Ireland, with sole responsibility for dealing with complaints about Gardaí. Under section 173 of the PSCS Act 2024, the Police Ombudsman is independent in the performance of their functions, including the investigation of cases and the operational organisation of Fiosrú. As Minister, I have no role in these matters. In 2025, Fiosrú established a Specialist Services Unit to investigate incidents, including public complaints, where a Garda is accused of domestic violence, coercive control, abuse of power for sexual purposes, child sexual abuse or sexual assault. The unit also investigates public complaints where it is alleged that a Garda failed to properly investigate incidents of this nature. The unit became operational in November 2025. The Unit investigates public complaints which have been determined by Fiosrú to be admissible and also Garda referrals of incidents involving Garda contact which have led to the death or serious harm of a member of the public. It should be noted that under the Act, serious harm includes an incident in which a person is the victim of a sexual offence or a victim of an abuse of power for a sexual purpose. Abuse of power for a sexual purpose means any behaviour by a Garda which takes advantage of their position to misuse their position, authority or powers for a sexual purpose or an improper emotional relationship with any other person. Since it became operational, the Unit’s staff have been allocated the following cases: • 12 investigations of domestic and sexual abuse where a Garda is an alleged perpetrator. Of these, eight are public complaints and four are investigations on foot of Garda referrals. • 23 investigations of domestic and sexual abuse where a Garda is alleged to have failed to properly deal with a report of domestic and sexual abuse. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the PSCS Act. The Commissioner is independent in the performance of his functions under section 34 of the Act. The Policing and Community Safety Authority (PCSA) was established in April 2025, following the commencement of the PSCS Act. The PCSA is an independent, statutory agency responsible for the oversight of An Garda Síochána. The core objective of the PCSA is to oversee and assess the performance of An Garda Síochána in relation to policing services, in an independent and transparent manner. By doing so, the PCSA supports the effective provision and continuous improvement of policing services in Ireland.
