question: 1988. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the Hammond Lane Courthouse; the actions taken to ensure its delivery; and the date when this much-needed and long-delayed facility will be open for use. [23240/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The construction of a purpose-built family law courts complex at Hammond Lane is a key priority for the Courts Service and is included in the National Development Plan. The new Dublin Family Courts Complex will be a modern purpose-built 19 courtroom facility where family law cases can be held in a dignified, secure and non-threatening environment with a range of support services to hand. It has been designed and will be built with the specific needs of Family Law court users in mind. The Family Courts complex at Hammond Lane will benefit families who interact with the courts at some of the most challenging junctures in their lives. Good progress is being made in delivering this much needed facility. Key achievements to date include: • Approval in principle to proceed with the project was granted by my Department in July 2023, following submission of a business case by the Courts Service as sponsoring agency. • Detailed plans/layouts for the building were developed by the OPW and approved by the Courts Service. The plans provide for a 6 storey over basement building providing approximately 18,250 sq m of purpose built accommodation. • Planning permission was granted by the Commissioners of Public Works in April 2024. • Technical and legal advisors were appointed by the National Development Finance Agency (NDFA) on behalf of the Courts Service in 2024. • The procurement process was initiated in July 2024. The project is being procured by the NDFA on behalf of the Courts Service in conjunction with the OPW, using the Competitive Dialogue procurement procedure pursuant to EU and national procurement law. • In November 2024 three candidates were pre-qualified to participate in the tender competition for the project. • Following preparation of the tender documents the project was formally handed over to the NDFA for procurement in accordance with the project governance arrangements in August 2025. On 28 August 2025, the NDFA issued the tender documentation to the three shortlisted candidates. The competitive dialogue phase of the procurement process is complete. The closing date for receipt of tenders was 25 March. Subject to the successful completion of the procurement process, it is envisaged that construction will commence in 2027.

question: 1989. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the actions being taken to combat the rise in homophobia in Ireland; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [23386/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Ireland is, in general, a diverse and welcoming country, but regrettably there is a small minority who subject others to intolerable abuse or attack resulting from their own prejudice. This behaviour cannot and will not be tolerated and anyone subjected to crimes motivated by homophobia should report it to An Garda Síochána who will investigate it. The National LGBTIQ+ Inclusion Strategy II 2024-2028 (NLIS II) and its associated two-year Action Plan 2025-2026, for which the Department of Children, Disability and Equality (DCDE) has responsibility, provides a roadmap towards equality for LGBTIQ+ people. The Strategy reflects a whole of Government commitment to fostering a safe, fair, and inclusive society for the LGBTIQ+ community. The Strategy takes a whole of lifecycle approach and has four key pillars: Safety; Health and Wellbeing; Participation and Inclusion; and Equality and Non-Discrimination. A key aim of NLIS II is to promote and respect the right of LGBTIQ+ people to live their lives safely, free of harassment and violence through several prevention and protection measures. This includes addressing misinformation in relation to LGBTIQ+ people; developing effective approaches within the criminal justice system towards addressing the safety issues experienced by the LGBTIQ+ community; addressing and preventing LGBTIQ+ bullying in schools; enhancing awareness of the occurrence of Domestic, Sexual and Gender Based Violence (DSGBV) within the LGBTIQ+ community and improving safety for LGBTIQ+ people in public spaces. If the Deputy has any additional questions in relation to the National LGBTIQ+ Inclusion Strategy II 2024-2028 (NLIS II), he may wish to put a question to the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality in this regard. My Department has also taken legislative action to protect those in vulnerable or minority communities. The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 came into force, in full, on 31 December 2024 and provides for increased prison sentences for certain offences, where they are proven to be motivated by hatred, or where hatred is demonstrated. For example, the legislation ensures that assault aggravated by hatred, or damage to property aggravated by hatred, will attract higher prison sentences. Where hatred is not proven, a person can still be charged with assault or damage to property. This ensures protections for victims, regardless of their background, if they are targeted because of certain identity characteristics, namely - sex characteristics and sexual orientation; race; colour; nationality; religion; national or ethnic origin; descent; disability; and gender. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána, which includes the training of Garda members and recruits and the allocation of resources. An Garda Síochána has a network of Garda Diversity Officers who have a specific role to engage and liaise with minority and diverse communities and advise them of the services available within An Garda Síochána. The Garda National Diversity Unit (GNDU) conduct monitoring of all Hate Crimes / Incidents, via PULSE and the media daily and where necessary assistance is offered to investigators to ensure incidents are correctly recorded and victims are afforded all necessary supports.

question: 1990. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way in which the closure of the Visitors Centre in Mountjoy Prison, which previously operated a family and child-friendly visiting space, aligns with the commitment in Young Ireland: the National Policy Framework for Children and Young People 2023 - 2028 to "establish a child-friendly visiting space in every prison in Ireland, and consult with children and families in the development and implementation of their policies on visiting." [24206/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Irish Prison Service (IPS) remains fully committed to the objectives set out in Young Ireland: The National Policy Framework for Children and Young People 2023–2028, including the specific commitment to ensure that prison visiting arrangements are child-centred, inclusive, and responsive to the needs of children and families impacted by imprisonment. The temporary closure of the standalone Visitors Centre at Mountjoy Prison represents a short-term, interim change in service delivery and provides an opportunity to reconfigure and modernise visiting facilities for Mountjoy Prison in line with Young Ireland’s framework objectives. At present, a temporary visitors reception area is in operation at the main gate on the North Circular Road at Mountjoy Prison. This arrangement was necessitated on health and safety grounds to facilitate essential construction works associated with the provision of additional female prisoner accommodation. This development is a critical measure to address overcrowding pressures within The Dóchas Centre. The temporary facility includes lockers, toilet facilities and baby-changing amenities. It is anticipated that a permanent visitors’ waiting facility will be reinstated as soon as possible, upon completion of the construction project. In line with the Young Ireland framework direction, the Irish Prison Service has developed proposals for a phased programme of upgrade and refurbishment of prison visitors’ centres nationally over the coming years. This programme is designed to ensure that all facilities provide dedicated, child-friendly visiting spaces that are welcoming, safe and non-intimidating, incorporate family-centred design principles, including appropriate seating, play areas and more informal, supportive environments. The Irish Prison Service is committed to ensuring that the visiting spaces are accessible and inclusive, with particular regard to the needs of children with disabilities and additional needs. The upgrade programme is informed by an increased awareness of neurodiversity and sensory needs, informed by research by the Irish Prison Service, AsIAm, University of Limerick and Trinity College Dublin. This includes, but is not exclusive to, the introduction of sensory-friendly spaces and quiet areas to support children who may experience sensory overload, appropriate lighting and reduced-noise environments and consideration of predictability and structure within visiting processes, which can be particularly beneficial for neurodivergent children. A national Expression of Interest process will shortly issue, seeking applications from organisations to operate prison visitors’ centres. From 2027, it is envisaged that these centres will also provide a range of evidence-based supports, including parenting support programmes, initiatives to strengthen family relationships, resilience-building supports for children of imprisoned parents and group support services for families. This approach reflects both national policy and international best practice, recognising that the quality of the visiting experience plays a critical role in maintaining family relationships and supporting the wellbeing of children affected by imprisonment.

question: 1991. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 1302 of 18 March 2026, if he will confirm the process for applying to view records; if that process is publicised online; and the number of researchers that have been facilitated under the scheme in the past ten years. [24209/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department is committed to ensuring access to its archives for researchers. To facilitate access to records which have not yet been transferred to the National Archives, the Records Management Unit of my Department regularly accommodates academics and researchers in Department offices to facilitate research projects requiring access to Department records. Individual researchers can contact my Department to request access to departmental records – such requests should be submitted in writing to info@justice.ie. In each case, Department officials carry out a search on records and where possible, grants access to records requested. There have been 20 such research requests facilitated since 2023.

question: 1992. Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to amend Stamp 3 restrictions on working to enable persons who are required to undertake a paid internship as part of a further or higher education course; the position of such persons; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24210/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can inform the Deputy that any non-EEA national student who is enrolled on a course or a Degree Programme from the Interim List of Eligible Programmes (ILEP), or eligible programmes offered by providers with authorisation to use the new TrustEd Education mark awarded by the Quality and Qualifications Ireland (QQI), is allowed to undertake an internship. However, this must form part of their course, contribute towards the final award, and cannot exceed 50% of the duration of the course. For those studying on a Stamp 3 immigration permission, an internship, once forming part of the course and contributing to the final course award, would be regarded as part of their studies and not considered employment. Similarly, for those studying on Stamp 2 immigration permission, an internship, where it is integral to a programme and regarded as part of their studies, would not be categorised as other employment and therefore does not affect the terms of the Stamp 2 permission. Colleges and educational institutions should provide a letter of confirmation to the student and their employer to show that the internship is part of a particular programme. The working hours and conditions while participating in the internship must be in accordance with employment law provisions. While all immigration permissions are kept under constant review, currently, there are no plans to make any amendments along the lines suggested by the Deputy.

question: 1993. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons with refugee status that are waiting over two years for family reunification; if any measures are being put in place to accelerate this process; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24240/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1993, 1994 and 1995 together. Family Reunification as provided for in Section 56 of the International Protection Act 2015, allows people granted international Protection status to apply for certain family members to join them in the State. Currently, an application for IP-FRU must be made by the sponsor within 12 months of them being granted an International Protection permission. I understand the wait times can be frustrating for applicants and their families. I want to assure anyone who has an application submitted that my Department remains committed to processing applications as efficiently as possible, while ensuring that each case is given the careful and thorough consideration required. I can advise the Deputy that that there are currently 589 family reunification applications on hand which are in excess of 24 months. It should be noted that no two applications are the same and processing times can vary depending on the nature of the application, the documentation supplied, and the detailed and often complex assessment that is required to be carried out on such applications. Where applications remain open for protracted periods this is predominantly due to factors outside of my Department's control; applicants frequently request that their applications are kept open as they seek more time to locate documents or the family members they wish to bring to the State. There are no specific arrangements in place to prioritise applications by reference to country of origin. Where applicants provide information indicating that there are particularly urgent or compelling circumstances, these are considered in the context of the individual case. In relation to the specific International Protection Family Reunification application referred to by the Deputy, this application has been received by my Department and continues to be processed at this time. All such applications are processed in chronological order, having regard to the individual circumstances of each case.

question: 1996. Deputy Michael Collins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total cost incurred by the State in opening, closing, reopening and now again closing an accommodation centre (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24254/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1996, 1997, 1998, 1999 and 2027 together. Details of payments made to specific providers for specific locations are not publicly supplied by my Department as such details are commercially sensitive. However, the Deputy may wish to note that payments over €20,000 to suppliers of the Department generally, including accommodation providers, are periodically published officially. The most recent figures can be found at the URL www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/collections/department-of-justice-purchase-orders-issued-over-20000-in-value/ Payments made prior to October 2025 may be found at the URL www.gov.ie/en/collection/dfdadb-department-of-children-and-youth-affairs-purchase-orders-for-20000-o / The property to which the Deputy refers had previously provided 90-Day accommodation from March 2024 to March 2025 for people fleeing the war in Ukraine. When this initial contract was due for renewal, there were sufficient beds available to the Department to meet the then lowering demand for 90-day accommodation and it was decided not to renew the contract for this accommodation. To address an increase in arrivals from Ukraine in late 2025, a new contract was agreed with this property for a three-month period from October 2025, which from 10 November 2025 operated under a new 30-day accommodation arrangement. The contract was extended to run until 14 April 2026, at which point it will cease to operate, due to falling numbers of arrivals from Ukraine. There were no additional costs incurred, such as contractual penalties, demobilisation costs or reinstatement works required. My Department aims to ensure that our portfolio of accommodation meets the evolving needs of the state’s response to the Ukraine Crisis. Two 30-day accommodation centres will remain in operation. The contracts will be monitored on an ongoing basis to ensuring value for money is obtained. Details of these centres is available at www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/designated-accommodation-centres/ The alternative housing proposals raised by the Deputy are not a matter for this Department. However, the Deputy may wish to note that accommodation is an exempt development within the meaning of SI 306/2022 (European Union (Planning and Development) (Displaced Persons from Ukraine Temporary Protection) Regulations 2022. This exemption does not apply to the use of the site to accommodate people other than people fleeing the war in Ukraine in receipt of temporary protection.

question: 2000. Deputy Rory Hearne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the national average number of Gardaí per 1,000 of the population; the number of Gardaí per 1,000 of the population in each Garda division and station, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2000 and 2151 together. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally. This includes a breakdown of Gardaí assigned by Garda Stations from 2009 to the end of February 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. Information for 2026 can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/garda-strength-breakdown-2026.html Information for previous years can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/december-2025.html The Deputy should select the most recently available date and then select the file titled ‘Garda Members by Division District Station" to access a breakdown of members assigned by Garda Division and Station.

question: 2001. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the timeline for when the transfer of functions on the Multi-Unit Developments Act 2011 will take place; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24281/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2001 and 2002 together. Under the Programme for Government, Securing Ireland’s Future, responsibility for the regulation of owner management companies (OMCs) and the Multi-Unit Development Act (MUDs) is to be transferred from my Department, to the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage. This will streamline support for OMCs and improve oversight. A timeline for the transfer of functions is currently being advanced and engagement between the Departments is ongoing in this regard. The transfer will initially be enabled by legislative amendments which are necessary to avoid a conflict of Ministerial responsibility as arose in the Mulcreevy case. These amendments are contained in the Criminal Law and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026 which has been referred to the Select Committee. The new housing action plan, ‘Delivering Homes, Building Communities: An Action Plan on Housing Supply and Targeting Homelessness’ which was published in November 2025 , commits the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage to undertake a review of the Act once the responsibility has transferred.

question: 2003. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to consider introducing a fee waiver for older applicants for Irish citizenship, as an elderly constituent, who has lived, worked and contributed Ireland since 1974 when they were 24 years and is of English nationality, cannot afford to access an Irish passport; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24287/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The fees payable in respect of applications for naturalisation are governed by the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Regulations 2011 (S.I. No. 569 of 2011). Currently, there is an application fee of €175 and a certification fee of €950 where an application is successful. A reduced certification fee of €200 applies in the case of an application made on behalf of a minor or in certain cases where the application is made by a widow, widower, or surviving civil partner of an Irish citizen. The State has not increased the fees for naturalisation applications since 2011. I have no plans at this time to introduce a waiver along the lines suggested by the Deputy.

question: 2007. Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of GoSafe speed detection vans currently in operation; the number deployed on a daily basis; and the comparison with 2019 and 2022 levels. [24342/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2007 and 2008 together. The whole of Government response to road safety is led by the Department of Transport and is a shared responsibility taken very seriously across Government. While the development and implementation of road traffic legislation and policy falls within the remit of my colleague the Minister for Transport, Darragh O'Brien, road traffic laws are enforced by Gardaí assigned to Roads Policing Units and as part of the day-to-day duties of uniformed Gardaí nationwide. Speeding remains one of the greatest risk factors on our roads. Speed reduces the time people have to react and makes collisions much more likely. It also makes it more likely that when collisions happen, they will lead to death or very serious injuries. Whether it is fixed cameras, average speed cameras or GoSafe vans, we need to use technology to work to reduce speeding on our roads. An Garda Síochána has contributed to making our roads safer through the use of mobile safety cameras, using service provider GoSafe to operate them on its behalf. I am informed by the Garda authorities that GoSafe currently have 58 mobile safety camera vans in operation, compared to 56 in 2019 and 55 in 2022. GoSafe are contracted to conduct an average of 9000 monitoring hours per calendar month, in comparison with 2019 and 2022 when the outsourced service provider were contracted to conduct an average of 7500 monitoring hours per calendar month. All mobile safety camera vans are fully deployed as per the service agreement. The mobile safety camera vans are only one part of a suite of measures used to enhance road safety for all road users. These measures include five average speed zones, nine static cameras, proactive enforcement by roads policing personnel together with enforcement by all operational Gardaí whom have a responsibility to address roads policing issues as they arise. In addition, An Garda Síochána is committed to having all operational uniform personnel perform a minimum 30 minutes of roads policing duties per tour of duty. question: 2015. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department or any other agencies under the aegis of his Department have made arrangements for the detention of persons arriving in the State for the purpose of applying for International Protection but who do not fulfil entry conditions; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24384/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2015, 2016 and 2017 together. My Department is focused on preparing for the implementation of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact in advance of 12 June 2026. The Pact will provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. The International Protection Bill 2026 will give effect to the measures of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. Enactment of the Bill and commencement of the Act is required by 12 June 2026. In line with the State’s obligations under the Reception Conditions Directive, the International Protection Bill 2026 provides for the use of detention only in certain exceptional and limited circumstances. The grounds for detention do not include or allow for the detention of an applicant for international protection solely on the basis that he or she does not fulfil conditions for entry to the State. Detention under the International Protection Bill 2026 will be for as short a time as possible and applicants will be informed of their right to seek free legal assistance and legal representation once they have been detained. A decision to detain an international protection applicant will be taken with the utmost seriousness and with due regard for the applicant’s fundamental rights. The intention of these provisions of the International Protection Bill 2026 is to ensure that applicants are treated fairly and humanely while also ensuring the effective and efficient operation of our international protection system.

question: 2020. question: 2021. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his views that the Data Protection commission has enough resources, statutory powers and backing to tackle the ongoing data security and related privacy issues facing the country, particularly in the lead up to the EU Presidency; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24441/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Data Protection Commission (DPC) is Ireland’s independent supervisory authority under the GDPR. Under the Data Protection Act 2018, the Commission is statutorily independent of the Government in the performance of its responsibilities and functions, as required by the GDPR. The Data Protection Commission plays a key role as one of the largest EU data protection authorities. As the lead supervisory authority in many cross-border cases, Ireland is often the first point of response for new and emerging data protection issues across the EU. The Government continues to invest significant resources to support the DPC to deliver on its evolving mandate. In 2025, the DPC was allocated a budget of €29.1 million, an increase of some 150% since 2018. The 2026 budget saw a further 10% increase to the budget of the DPC, with an additional €3 million to support increased staffing. Having regard to the expanding role of the DPC in the digital regulatory environment and its organisational structure, governance and business needs, the Government decided on 27 July 2022 to move to a three Commissioner model, as provided for under the Data Protection Act 2018. Commissioners, Dr. Des Hogan and Mr. Dale Sunderland were appointed in February 2024 and the Government appointed a third Commissioner, Ms Niamh Sweeney, on 13th October 2025, following an open competition run by Public Jobs. The digital regulatory environment is advancing at pace, and this new three Commissioner model reflects the increased workload for the Commission arising from the suite of the EU’s new digital legislation, including the EU AI Act, the Data Act, the Political Advertising Regulation and the Platform Workers Directive. I have full confidence that the DPC will continue to perform its vital role. Published statistics, which include Human Resources, are available in the DPC’s most recent annual report, available at the following link: Data Protection Commission Annual Report 2024. A more detailed breakdown, if required, can be sought via the DPC’s dedicated Oireachtas email address oireachtasqueries@dataprotection.ie.

question: 2022. Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether any artificial intelligence tools or systems are currently being used within his Department or in agencies under its remit; the purposes for which these tools are being used; whether any departmental guidance or governance structures have been developed to support their responsible use; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24462/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can confirm that there are artificial intelligence (AI) tools currently in use within my Department, primarily in the area of immigration services. My Department’s Immigration Service Delivery operates a Digital Contact Centre, which includes an AI enabled smart assistant and chatbot powered by Microsoft Copilot. This system assists users in navigating publicly available immigration information, checking application status, booking appointments, and submitting queries. The chatbot is trained exclusively on information published on the Immigration Service Delivery website, operates within a secure authenticated portal, and does not process or make decisions based on personal data. More complex issues can be referred to staff at any stage. In addition, the Department uses ID Pal, which employs machine learning based identity verification to authenticate applicants’ identity documents when establishing a customer account within the same service portal. My Department complies with the Guidelines for the Responsible Use of AI in the Public Service issued by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, as well as guidance from the National Cyber Security Centre. The Department is fully committed to transparency, including informing users whenever they are interacting with an AI system. My Department has put in place appropriate governance, risk assessment and oversight structures to support the responsible use of these technologies. My Department will continue to assess emerging digital tools, including AI, but any future adoption will remain subject to appropriate governance processes, including risk assessment and human oversight. With regards to the use of AI tools in agencies under the aegis of my Department, I am informed of the following. Fiosrú’s Digital Investigations Unit use various software products that contain AI-powered algorithms, machine learning and neural networks to automate actions for later manual review and confirmation by a human operator, such as high-volume screening and video redaction tasks. All AI components used are on isolated on-prem installations with no external link to the internet. All output is manually reviewed and confirmed by a human operator. No AI-based software modules are used for digital or audio/visual forensic processing or examination work at Fiosrú. The Legal Aid Board is at an early stage in its engagement with AI tools. Current use is limited to low risk, internal support functions and is governed by the Board’s Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework. No AI tools are used in decision making, eligibility assessments, or the provision of legal advice or representation. All access to justice decisions remains the responsibility of appropriately qualified staff. The Courts Service, Judicial Council and Policing and Community Safety Authority have access to Microsoft Co-pilot, which is utilised as a general-purpose AI tool to assist with non-automated administrative tasks under human oversight. This is part of a suite of Microsoft 365 products available alongside other MS software and tools. The Data Protection Commission is conducting a pilot project to explore the use of AI. This project is limited to a small set of users using only publicly available/non-sensitive data. While no AI tools are currently in use in An Garda Síochána, I am informed that work is underway to develop a strategy for the deployment of AI within the organisation and to establish robust governance structures in relation to the use of such emerging technologies.

question: 2023. Deputy Liam Quaide asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will engage with the Central Statistics Office to prioritise urgent data collection needs relating to AI-generated sexual abuse imagery; if he will request the CSO to bring forward their sexual violence survey as soon as possible to collect urgently needed data relating to technology-facilitated sexual abuse. [24466/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2023, 2024 and 2025 together. New developments and issues in artificial intelligence are something the Government is very conscious of and these matters are being considered across Government, including by the Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, Niamh Smyth. My Department is currently in the process of developing a new Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence (DSGBV) survey with CUAN and the Central Statistics Office (CSO). This new survey will be based on the EU Gender-Based Violence (EU-GBV) survey, which will be carried out in most EU member states next year under the direction of Eurostat. This new CSO survey will provide statistics on the forms of violence experienced by women and men in Ireland, including physical, sexual, economic, psychological and technology-facilitated abuse and will also capture information about the contexts and relationships within which the violence occurs. The CSO is currently working with stakeholders drawn from service providers and academia, to develop the content of the survey, and ensure that the statistics it produces will meet national data and policy needs, while also being comparable internationally. The content and design of the survey will also be informed by the report of a national advisory group on Domestic Violence and Abuse commissioned by CUAN in 2025. The questionnaire for the new DSGBV survey will be developed and tested later this year via a series of focus group meetings with victims and survivors, and there will also be a pilot field test in Quarter 4 of this year. Following this development process, the survey is expected to 'go-live' in late-2027 across all countries in Europe with results available in 2028. Final decisions about the content of the questionnaire, the design of the survey and the statistics arising from it are the responsibility of the CSO, which is an independent agency operating under the Statistics Act 1993.

question: 2027. Deputy Michael Collins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if consideration will be given to repurposing an accommodation centre (details supplied), previously used for Ukrainian temporary protection accommodation, for alternative urgent housing needs, specifically for the provision of temporary accommodation for persons experiencing homelessness and for essential key workers such as hospital staff, members of An Garda Síochána and teachers who are working in the area on a temporary basis; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24493/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1996, 1997, 1998, 1999 and 2027 together. Details of payments made to specific providers for specific locations are not publicly supplied by my Department as such details are commercially sensitive. However, the Deputy may wish to note that payments over €20,000 to suppliers of the Department generally, including accommodation providers, are periodically published officially. The most recent figures can be found at the URL www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/collections/department-of-justice-purchase-orders-issued-over-20000-in-value/ Payments made prior to October 2025 may be found at the URL www.gov.ie/en/collection/dfdadb-department-of-children-and-youth-affairs-purchase-orders-for-20000-o / The property to which the Deputy refers had previously provided 90-Day accommodation from March 2024 to March 2025 for people fleeing the war in Ukraine. When this initial contract was due for renewal, there were sufficient beds available to the Department to meet the then lowering demand for 90-day accommodation and it was decided not to renew the contract for this accommodation. To address an increase in arrivals from Ukraine in late 2025, a new contract was agreed with this property for a three-month period from October 2025, which from 10 November 2025 operated under a new 30-day accommodation arrangement. The contract was extended to run until 14 April 2026, at which point it will cease to operate, due to falling numbers of arrivals from Ukraine. There were no additional costs incurred, such as contractual penalties, demobilisation costs or reinstatement works required. My Department aims to ensure that our portfolio of accommodation meets the evolving needs of the state’s response to the Ukraine Crisis. Two 30-day accommodation centres will remain in operation. The contracts will be monitored on an ongoing basis to ensuring value for money is obtained. Details of these centres is available at www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/designated-accommodation-centres/ The alternative housing proposals raised by the Deputy are not a matter for this Department. However, the Deputy may wish to note that accommodation is an exempt development within the meaning of SI 306/2022 (European Union (Planning and Development) (Displaced Persons from Ukraine Temporary Protection) Regulations 2022. This exemption does not apply to the use of the site to accommodate people other than people fleeing the war in Ukraine in receipt of temporary protection.

question: 2033. Deputy Ged Nash asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to extend the common travel area to people who have valid visas to enter the UK; if he has given any consideration to this matter recently; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24781/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2033 and 2034 together. The Common Travel Area (CTA) facilitates Irish and British citizens to move and reside freely across Ireland and the UK while maintaining access for citizens to a range of reciprocal rights and privileges central to everyday life. The CTA arrangements apply only to Irish and British citizens. While there is excellent cooperation on CTA matters, the immigration rules that apply in the UK and Ireland are a matter for each jurisdiction. The UK authorities do not issue residence permissions which identify the UK location of the holder. For example, it is not possible to distinguish a Third Country National (TCN) living in Belfast from a TCN living in Manchester based on the production of their UK eVisa. Accordingly, a person who requires a visa to enter the State must hold a valid Irish visa, regardless of any immigration permission they may hold in the UK, including where travelling from Northern Ireland. Nationals who are subject to Irish Visa requirements (both short stay and long stay), as set out in Orders made under section 17 (1) of the Immigration Act 2004 (as amended), are required to be in possession of the appropriate visa when seeking entry to the State. This includes TCNs resident in the UK including Northern Ireland. CTA cooperation has brought benefits for certain groups of visa required nationals in respect of the Short Stay Visa Waiver programme and the British Irish Visa Scheme. Any visa required visitor to the UK wishing to also visit Ireland may consider the Short Stay Visa Waiver Programme (SSVWP). This allows nationals of certain countries, who have entered the UK on foot of certain UK short stay visas, to travel to Ireland without the requirement to obtain an Irish visa. Details of this programme are available on my Department's website here: www.irishimmigration.ie/coming-to-visit-ireland/short-stay-visa-waiver-programme/ . It is open to any person with the requisite travel history to apply for a multi entry visa. The London Visa Office processes visa applications from people with a residence permission in the United Kingdom including Northern Ireland for short stay purposes (less than 90 days) such as Tourism, Business, family visits, and to use Dublin Airport to transit onwards to other destinations or as part of their return journey to the UK.

This allows nationals of certain countries, who have entered the UK on foot of certain UK short stay visas, to travel to Ireland without the requirement to obtain an Irish visa. Details of this programme are available on my Department's website here: www.irishimmigration.ie/coming-to-visit-ireland/short-stay-visa-waiver-programme/ . It is open to any person with the requisite travel history to apply for a multi entry visa. The London Visa Office processes visa applications from people with a residence permission in the United Kingdom including Northern Ireland for short stay purposes (less than 90 days) such as Tourism, Business, family visits, and to use Dublin Airport to transit onwards to other destinations or as part of their return journey to the UK.

question: 2035. Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on a citizenship application for a person (details supplied). [24830/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department. This application is based on Section 16 'Irish Association', which can take longer to process than applications based upon residency. Section 15 of the Act sets out the statutory conditions that must be fulfilled for a certificate of naturalisation to be granted. Section 16 of the Act gives discretion to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or Irish associations (related through blood, affinity or adoption to a person who is or is entitled to be an Irish citizen). Last year my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. They set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-a-citizen/. Applicants can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 2036. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of international protection applicants who have undergone an age assessment at the International Protection Office; the outcomes of those assessments; details of the appeals process and outcomes of appeals; the qualifications, experience and training of staff carrying out the assessments; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24863/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Under the provisions of the International Protection Act 2015, Section 14 requires the International Protection Office (IPO) to refer an unaccompanied minor to Tusla. Tusla then carry out an assessment for eligibility for services under the Childcare Acts. Where Tusla find that the applicant is not an unaccompanied minor (UAM), the applicant is returned to the IPO to make their application as an adult. It remains open to the applicant to request a re-assessment based on submission of a valid form of identity which supports these assertions. Historically, a practice built up where if an individual presented for asylum and claimed to be a minor, they were generally referred to Tusla, with the IPO accepting Tusla’s determination of whether or not an individual was entitled to access their services as a proxy for an age assessment process. The new International Protection Bill 2026 will give effect to the measures of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. Enactment of the Bill and commencement of the Act is required by 12 June 2026. The Bill brings additional safeguards into the age assessment process such as the appointment of a representative to the applicant and additional assessment criteria underage assessment such as a psychosocial assessment. Under the Pact, • Where age cannot be established, a presumption of minority will apply and the applicant will be referred to Tusla, as soon as possible. • The Department will complete an age assessment on applicants claiming to be an UAM. The assessment will be multidisciplinary, carried out by trained professionals and use the least invasive methods available. This process is currently being designed and Tusla are represented on the working group carrying out this design work. • Those who claim to be an UAM will be assigned a representative who will assist them throughout screening, including, where applicable, the age assessment process. The role of such a representative will also be to assist and guide the individual through the international protection application process with a view to safeguarding the best interests of the child and, in particular, to assist with the lodging of the application for international protection and the personal interview. As part of preparations for the implementation of the Pact, elements of the processes related to UAMs are currently being introduced on a phased basis. These include engaging with applicants who claim to be minors to assess their age (e.g. considering what they say about their background, family, education, travel arrangements and reviewing any documentation produced) with referrals to Tusla only being made once the International Protection Officer is satisfied that the individual is under 18. As was previously the case, if Tusla find that the applicant is not an unaccompanied minor, they are returned to the IPO to make their application as an adult. The applicant is provided with a decision in writing which outlines the reasons for the decision along with details on how to appeal the decision. Where the results of the assessment are inconclusive, the applicant is given the benefit of the doubt and is referred to Tusla who provide services under the Childcare Acts. Where the IPO find that the applicant is an UAM, they are referred to Tusla who provide services under the Childcare Act. The IPO have referred 26 applicants to Tusla since 1st January 2026. Since the introduction of the Pact transition process in February, 10 applicants who have claimed to be UAMs have been deemed to be adults by the IPO. There are 6 appeals on hand, all of which have been scheduled for assessment under Section 24, International Protection Act 2015. The staff conducting age assessments at the International Protection Office are experienced front line immigration officers who have completed appropriate training. They will complete further tailored training in advance of the commencement of the International Protection Bill 2026 in June.

question: 2037. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the IPAT recognition rate for each year from 2021-2025 inclusive, for safe countries and standard cases; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24864/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration There has been a significant increase in investment into the international protection system which, combined with digitisation and process reengineering, has facilitated a major increase in processing capacity. In 2025, the International Protection Office (IPO) delivered over 20,200 first decisions compared to approximately 14,100 in 2024: a 44% increase. The International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) more than doubled the number of appeals closed from 3,100 in 2024 to nearly 6,300 in 2025. All applications for international protection are considered on an individual basis. As a result, refusal and grant rates can increase and decrease without a clear trend, depending on the applications that are under consideration at any particular time. I can inform the Deputy that under section 72 of the International Protection Act, I, as Minister may make an order designating a country as a safe country of origin. This designation means it can be shown that there is generally no persecution, torture or inhuman or degrading treatment, or threat of violence from an armed conflict in that country. This assessment is based on a range of sources of information, including from other EU Member States, the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA), the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, the Council of Europe, and other international organisations as appropriate. Ireland currently has fifteen countries designated as safe countries of origin: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Georgia, Montenegro, Kosovo, Serbia, South Africa, Botswana, Algeria, Brazil, Egypt, India, Malawi and Morocco. All applicants refused international protection have a right to appeal to the International Protection Appeals Tribunal who must then consider if the earlier International Protection Office determinations on refugee status and subsidiary protection should be affirmed or set aside. The table below shows the decisions made for standard cases by the International Protection Appeals Tribunal from 2021 to 2025. Year Decisions Total Decision % Granted/Set Aside Refused/Affirmed Granted/Set Aside Refused/Affirmed 2021 332 492 824 40% 60% 2022 423 534 957 44% 56% 2023 339 668 1,007 34% 66% 2024 545 817 1,362 40% 60% 2025 1,045 2,278 3,323 31% 69% The table below shows the decisions made for Safe Countries by the International Protection Appeals Tribunal from 2021 to 2025. Year Decisions Grand Total Decision % Granted/Set Aside Refused/Affirmed Granted/Set Aside Refused/Affirmed 2021 53 175 228 23% 77% 2022 73 270 343 21% 79% 2023 107 468 575 19% 81% 2024 274 1,234 1,508 18% 82% 2025 443 1,738 2,181 20% 80% Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. My Department continues to focus on preparing for the EU Migration and Asylum Pact in advance of June 2026. The Pact will provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through convergence in asylum practices across the EU. A new appeals body, the Tribunal for Asylum and Returns Appeals (TARA), will replace the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT).

question: 2038. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of vulnerability assessments carried out each month from January 2025 to present; the number of adults and children assessed; the number of those assessed as vulnerable; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24865/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration When a person applies for international protection, their needs are assessed by IPAS, in line with S.I. No. 230/2018 - European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018 . This vulnerability assessment checks if people have special reception needs, and if so, the nature of those needs. The regulations define a broad set of categories of vulnerability. They include any person who is a minor, an unaccompanied minor, a person with a disability, an elderly person, a pregnant woman, any single parent of a minor, a victim of human trafficking, a person with a serious illness or medical condition, a person with a mental disorder and a person who has been subjected to torture, rape or other form of serious psychological physical or sexual violence. In addition to these categories, IPAS gives consideration to persons who are LGBTQ+. A voluntary vulnerability assessment programme is in place to assess special reception needs. Taking part in the assessment is voluntary. Where a vulnerability is identified, the person is signposted to relevant services, and information is also used by IPAS to appropriately accommodate people. It is important to note that the majority of vulnerabilities can be addressed in any IPAS accommodation. The vulnerability assessment programme was paused during 2024 due to very significant increases in application numbers that had been seen from 2022 onward. The programme recommenced in November 2024, when family applicants were offered assessments, and from June 2025, the programme was expanded further to include all family and single female applicants. question: 2040. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide a list of community service orders issued in the DMR North region. [24869/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2040 and 2041 together. I am advised by the Probation Service that they cannot provide specific information on Community Service Orders in the DMR North region as this is a Garda divisional district area and the Probation Service works on a county-by-county basis. However, I can inform the Deputy that 332 Community Service Orders were made throughout County Dublin in 2024, the latest year for which annual figures have been published. Community Service Orders are made in lieu of, and as an alternative to, a custodial sentence. The Probation Service has overall responsibility to assess, manage and supervise the performance of a Community Service Order. Detailed procedures are in place to manage compliance. The Criminal Justice (Community Service) Act 1983 as amended by Criminal Justice (Community Service) (Amendment) Act 2011 currently provides for Community Service Orders between 40-240 hours. Failure to comply with the Order is an offence and the Probation Service will prosecute in cases of non-compliance. Compliance is managed through an approach encompassing client accountability, support and encouragement, formal record keeping, oversight from the Community Service Supervisors and acknowledgement of successful completion of Order to both clients and the Courts. Non-compliance is addressed through a system of formal warnings. Every effort is made to support and re-engage clients where difficulties emerge. When all efforts are exhausted, matters will be returned to Court by the Probation Service. Revocation of a Community Service Order may result in the imposition of the alternative prison sentence. This is a matter for the Court to determine.

question: 2042. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the average time period for a Garda vetting application to take place; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24883/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau (GNVB) is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. This requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. The Garda National Vetting Bureau received 633,563 applications for vetting disclosures in 2025 and completed 596,975 applications during the same period. In respect of current processing timeframes I am advised by the Garda National Vetting Bureau that the current processing time for 85% of vetting applications is 8/9 working days. It should be noted that in a number of instances, it is necessary to conduct enquiries with Garda Stations and external agencies such as the Courts Service, Probation Service, and Tusla (the Child and Family Agency), etc. These enquiries are conducted for a multiplicity of reasons such as verification of identity; updating of incomplete records; and establishing outcomes of investigations. In such instances, processing times are significantly longer than the general average. Vetting can also take longer where a person has spent time living abroad.

question: 2044. Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason applicants for Irish Citizenship through the INIS online portal are only given one opportunity to submit requested additional documentation/information during the application process, given that applications where a query is raised and the requested documentation submitted and which are subsequently refused are not given another opportunity to submit additional documentation and there is no appeal process in relation to applications for naturalisation under the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956,; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24896/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can inform the Deputy that my Department has produced a comprehensive guidance document for all potential applicants for naturalisation, outlining all the documents required for an application. This document is published on my Department's Immigration website and is available here: www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Citizenship-Guidance-Document-April-2024.pdf All applicants should take care to submit all the required supporting documentation with their application. Where my Department identifies an incomplete application, they will afford the applicant 28 days to provide the missing documents. Although there is no appeal option provided for under the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, it is open to anyone to make a new application at any time. There is no time limit within which you can make a new application, nor is there any maximum limit on the number of applications. Applicants are advised that in making any new application they should bear in mind the reasons why the previous application was deemed ineligible. Detailed information on how to apply for naturalisation and other resources is available here: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-a-citizen/.

question: 2045. answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes all operational and investigative policing matters, including decisions regarding the allocation and deployment of Garda members and resources throughout the State. I would like to refer the Deputy to Parliamentary Question 180 of 18 March 2026 in which the matters raised in respect of requesting Aid to a Civil Power were addressed by the Minister for Defence.

question: 2049. Deputy Keira Keogh asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of prosecutions for dog fouling in Ireland in 2025; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [24975/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2049 and 2050 together. Under the Litter Pollution Act, 1997, the primary responsibility for management and enforcement responses to litter pollution lies with local authorities. It is a matter for each local authority to determine the most appropriate public awareness, enforcement, and clean-up actions in relation to litter taking account of local circumstances and priorities. Prosecutions are a matter for the Director of Prosecutions (DPP), who is fully independent in her functions. As Minister, I have no role in the operations, functions, governance or oversight of the Office of the DPP and I am unable to provide any information or statistics relating to the Director's work as a result. Additionally, management of the courts, along with related operational matters and logistical functions, are the responsibility of the judiciary and Courts Service, which are independent in exercising their functions under the Courts Service Act 1998 and through the separation of powers in the Constitution. The Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Houses of the Oireachtas: oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie.

question: 2051. question: 2053. Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of civil and public servants in his Department and agencies under its remit who have received training in AI, data literacy, or digital skills in the past year; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [25039/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration In order to assist in achieving its strategic objectives, my Department is fully committed to enhancing the capacity and capability of staff and provides access to a full programme of learning & development resources to meet the needs of both staff and the organisation. By providing appropriate supports and encouraging staff to take ownership of their own development, my Department promotes a culture of learning and continuous professional development in line with business needs. My Department provides a central learning and development offering via the digital platform OneLearning. OneLearning provides the core, essential skills and capabilities for the Civil Service. This includes self-paced and virtual learning programmes, which includes training on AI, data literacy and digital skills. In addition, my Department considers additional training requests when there is a business case provided to support the request, and which cannot be met via OneLearning. The need identified should support or enhance the staff member(s) performance in their current role, their work area and/or the Department. The information requested by the Deputy is presented in the attached appendix. question: 2054. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of deaths linked to gender-based and sexual violence recorded in each of the past ten years. [25072/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The collation and publication of crime stats are a matter for the Central Statistics Office (CSO). The CSO is the national statistics agency, established under the Statistics Act 1993. Under section 13 of the Statistics Act 1993, the Central Statistics Office (CSO) is fully independent in its role of publishing statistics, and the standards applied to these statistics. Further to this, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. This includes all operational policing and security matters, including the analysis of crime trends. Furthermore, under section 34(1) of the Policing Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is independent in the performance of his functions. I have no responsibility in relation to these independent functions. To be of assistance to the Deputy, I have made enquiries with An Garda Síochána who advise that there is no specific field or incident type by which incidents of Domestic, Sexual and Gender Based violence can be identified. I am informed that AGS can provide figures on domestic abuse Incidents which is outlined in their thematic report on [ ]Domestic, Sexual and Gender Based Violence published in 2022 and available at - www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/office-of-corporate-communications/news-media/an-garda-siochana-domestic-sexual-and-gender-based-violence-report-sept-22.pd f The report focused on incidents reported between 2019 and 2021, and longer term trends back to 2013 were also included. question: 2059. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to introduce specific legislation to address the creation and distribution of AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery, including child sexual abuse material; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [25111/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 2059 and 2063 together. New developments and issues in artificial intelligence are something the Government is very conscious of and these matters are being considered across Government, including by the Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, Niamh Smyth. It is important to note that there is a significant body of legislation already in place dealing with online creation, publication and distribution of images. Under the Digital Services Act, the European Commission is responsible for the oversight of very large online platforms. These platforms are required to assess and mitigate risks that their services may create in relation to the proliferation of illegal content online and the protection of fundamental rights, including protection for minors. The EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act introduces legal requirements that aim to ensure a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights against the harmful effects of AI systems in the European Union. Under the AI Act, certain AI practices are prohibited, and certain AI systems and uses of AI by providers and deployers are subject to legal requirements in terms of governance, transparency and responses to risks and incidents. Responsibility for the legislation that provides for Coimisiún na Meán’s role in respect of regulation of online safety – the Online Safety Media Regulation Act 2022 – is with the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport. That Act is the basis for the Online Safety Code. The requirements of this code are drawn from the Act, along with the EU Digital Services Act and the EU Terrorist Content Online Regulation. The Online Safety Code places a requirement on service providers to demonstrate that they have the correct safety measures in place to prevent illegal or harmful content on their platforms. The Harassment, Harmful Communications and Related Offences Act 2020 (Coco’s Law) created a serious offence of the distribution or publication of an intimate image without consent with intent to cause harm to the victim, attracting a maximum penalty of up to 7 years imprisonment. It is also an offence to threaten to distribute or publish such an image. The Act also provides for a strict liability offence, with a lower penalty, for engaging in the recording, distribution or publication of an intimate image without consent, with no requirement to prove an intention to cause harm. The definition of an intimate image under the 2020 Act is intentionally broad to include any visual representation of a person. This is to include intimate images which have been altered or doctored prior to their distribution or publication, more commonly referred to as ‘deep fakes’. Similarly, the Child Trafficking and Pornography Act 1998 is framed so that no distinction can be made between AI-generated material and other child sexual abuse material. ‘Child pornography’ as defined in the Act includes “reference to a figure resembling a person that has been generated or modified by computer-graphics or otherwise”. The production and distribution of child sexual abuse material attracts a sentence of up to 14 years imprisonment. The EU Violence Against Women Directive provides a comprehensive framework to effectively prevent and combat violence against women and domestic violence. The Directive includes a provision which criminalises the creation and distribution of deepfake images. Work is underway in the Department to transpose the Directive. Following the commencement of the Harassment, Harmful Communications and Related Offences Act 2020, the Department of Justice launched and ran a two-stage campaign to raise awareness of Intimate Image Abuse and to better inform people of the new offences within the act place to combat it. In September 2021, the first phase of the campaign, called ‘The Chain of Shame’ focused on the sharing of intimate images without consent. It highlighted that it was now a criminal offence regardless of the motivation for sharing and provided information for victims about reporting it to An Garda Síochána for investigation and/or to Hotline.ie to have the image(s) taken down from the internet. 'The Chain of Shame' began as an online and digital only campaign but was later expanded into a major national multimedia campaign designed to reach a national audience. The second phase of the campaign, called ‘Serious Consequences’ launched in May 2023 and focused on raising awareness that it is also illegal to threaten to share an intimate image of another person, even if the threat is not followed through. Serious Consequences ran across TV, local and national radio, digital audio, video on demand, digital out of home screens and in cinemas. This two staged approach was highly successful in raising awareness of the new offences relating to intimate image abuse. Prior to the launch of the campaign only 51% of people thought it is against the law in Ireland to threaten to share intimate images without consent, that figure has now risen to 96%. Knowledge of the offence of actually sharing without consent rose from 69% to 97%.

question: 2060. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures in place to mitigate risks of bias and false positives in facial recognition and biometric AI systems to be used by An Garda Síochána; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [25112/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am advised that An Garda Síochána ICT have not deployed any artificial intelligence (AI) systems for use across the organisation. Garda authorities are working closely with officials in my Department in respect of the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) (Amendment) Bill. This Bill aims to provide a clear legal basis to support the introduction of new advanced processing techniques, that utilise AI to enable faster analysis of video footage for the purposes of an investigation, including through the use of biometric technology. Prior to any change in AI use by An Garda Síochána, the initial focus will be to develop the strategy for the deployment of AI within the organisation and to establish robust governance structures in relation to the use of such emerging technologies. Any future policing solution deployed by An Garda Síochána that may have AI features embedded will be managed by a robust system with Role Based Access Control (RBAC) where tools will not be available unless the situation warrants them. Also, any AI functionality will only be used as a tool to aid investigations and no decision that produces an adverse legal effect for an individual will be based solely on automated processing. AI systems deployed by An Garda Síochána will be subject to human oversight. In terms of False Positives and bias, all AI capable systems will be treated as decision support systems, where a layered system of safeguards are in place, including algorithmic tuning undertaken by senior investigators, and a process of human review of all decisions taken as part of investigations. A new code of practice under the Recording Devices (Amendment) Bill will be required for guidelines and senior member oversight is integral to making any decision.

question: 2061. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current staffing levels and resourcing of the Garda National Cyber Crime Bureau; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [25113/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State, including to specialist units, in accordance with the Policing Security and Community Safety Act 2024. I regularly engage with the Commissioner to ensure that he has the resources that he needs, however, as Minister I have no role in these independent functions. I am advised Garda authorities that as of 28 February, the latest date for when figures are available, there were 73 Gardai assigned to the GNCCB, including 56 Garda members, 12 Sergeants, two Inspectors, two Superintendents, and a Chief Superintendent. The Government is committed to ensuring that An Garda Síochána has the resources it needs to fight all types of crime, including cybercrime. The 2026 allocation provides a record budget of over €2.74 billion to An Garda Síochána.

question: 2062. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the steps being taken to counter the use of AI-generated deepfakes in scams, impersonation offences and potential election interference; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [25115/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The rate of development in AI tools is unprecedented. A whole of Government approach is required to address AI challenges effectively and harness AI opportunities. My Department has engaged, and continues to engage, with counterparts across other Departments on digital matters, including AI. The Minister of State for Trade Promotion, Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation, Niamh Smyth, is the first Minister of State to hold a portfolio concerning AI. The Department of Enterprise led the negotiations on the AI Act and is leading on its implementation at a national level. There is no stand-alone provision under Irish law that provides that identity theft/fraud constitutes an offence, however it is addressed through a combination of legislative measures, primarily the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud) Offences Act 2001 and the Criminal Justice (Offences Relating to Information Systems) Act 2017. Section 6(1) of the 2001 Act provides a broad offence of making gain or causing loss by deception which can be applied to the fraudulent use of another person's identity. This can capture a range of identity-based misconduct where deception results in financial or personal gain. For instance, using stolen identity details to open a bank account or access credit can fall under this provision. While acts like phishing may not be specific offences in themselves, they can be prosecuted where they form part of a wider deceptive scheme that meets the criteria of this section. This is supplemented by the Criminal Justice (Offences Relating to Information Systems) Act 2017, which was introduced to address cybercrime and related offences, such as unauthorised access to systems, data interference, and the use of malware. While the 2017 Act does not create a specific offence of identity theft, it recognises the seriousness of identity misuse by considering it as an aggravating factor for an offence under s.3 (Interference with information system without lawful authority) or s.4 (Interference with data without lawful authority). Section 8(4)(a) provides for this, dealing with offences such as data interference committed using false personal data, where the court is required to treat this as grounds for imposing a more severe penalty. My Department and I are committed to continuing our active engagement and collaboration with our counterparts across Government to ensure we address the challenge posed by AI.
